# Introduction

This is the second book in the Do-It-Yourself Java Games series. The first book's programs were text-based so you could develop basic Java programming skills. With that background, you should be ready for the next level of programming: Java [graphics](#part0003_split_082.html_graphics) and [event-driven programming](#part0003_split_082.html_event-driven-programming). Java graphics add color and images to games. But what is event-driven programming?

An event-driven program creates an initial screen, then waits for the program user to take an action. The user may click a [button](#part0003_split_082.html_button), click on an image, drag something, or press a key on the keyboard. The program then responds to that action; whatever that action may be. Writing such a program is called event-driven programming.

The event-driven programs in this book will teach you how to respond to user input from:

*   [Windows](#part0003_split_082.html_window) and [dialogs](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog)
*   Buttons and [input fields](#part0003_split_082.html_input-field)
*   Images and drawings
*   [Keyboard input](#part0003_split_082.html_keyboard-input)
*   Mouse clicks and drags

As in the previous book in this series, the lessons in each project are presented using a “try-it” approach: do the steps shown and see what happens. You'll be given programming tasks, each followed by a program [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) [listing](#part0003_split_082.html_listing). The listings have fill-in blanks to allow you to write much of the program code yourself. But don't worry if you're unsure of how to fill in the blanks; simply click the completed listing's link to see the missing code.

Don't skip any lessons. Each lesson explains a new programming technique, which may be used again in later lessons. Doing all the lessons will make later lessons easier.

[*Appendix A - Glossary*](#part0003_split_081.html_Appendix-A---Glossary) has definitions of Java programming terms and links to more information. The first use of each term, like “graphics” and “event-driven programming” used above, will include a [clickable](#part0003_split_082.html_clickable) link to the word in the glossary.

Several different approaches can often accomplish the same programming task. You don't have to use the code shown in the answer if your code does what was asked or if you prefer your code's results. Feel free to experiment with the code and see what happens. Half the fun of programming is making programs do what you want them to do.

The *Do-It-Yourself Java Games* books are designed for e-readers. Click the image below or follow this [link](http://youtu.be/XMuXNyyk7mg) to watch a video showing the features in these electronic books that would not be possible in a print book.

[![](images/00002.jpeg)](http://youtu.be/XMuXNyyk7mg)

More Do-It-Yourself Java Games was updated to a second edition to work in Windows 10 and Java 8, and to make sure the games will run as designed across multiple platforms, including Windows, OS X, and Linux.

## The Programs

You'll create ten computer programs that use graphics and event-driven programming:

### Wizard of Yes/No

![](images/00003.jpeg)

Learn how to create a window, add text, change [fonts](#part0003_split_082.html_font), and add [scroll bars](#part0003_split_082.html_scroll-bars).

The Wizard of Yes/No can help with making yes or no decisions.

### Guess My Color

![](images/00004.jpeg)

Learn the basics of Java [color](#part0003_split_082.html_color), window [layout](#part0003_split_082.html_layout), and clickable buttons as you build this game.

The goal of Guess My Color is to match the target color by adjusting the red, green, and blue hue of the sample color.

### Framed

![](images/00005.jpeg)

Learn to customize buttons that change appearance when clicked.

Clicking tiles in Framed will turn groups of lights on or off. The goal is to form a frame of lights.

### Watch Your Step

![](images/00006.jpeg)

Learn to customize buttons that display color or text, considering the state of the button.

The goal in Watch Your Step is to reveal all the safe terrain tiles without stepping on a black hole. The numbers show how many neighboring tiles have holes.

### Sliding Tiles

![](images/00007.jpeg)

Learn to create a [menu bar](#part0003_split_082.html_menu-bar) and work with images as you build this game of sliding tiles.

The object of Sliding Tiles is to unscramble the picture by sliding the tiles back to their original positions.

### Maze Generator: Maze and Anti-Maze

![](images/00008.jpeg) ![](images/00009.jpeg)

Learn to paint circles, lines, and rectangles as you draw the parts of a maze. You'll also learn to respond to [keystroke](#part0003_split_082.html_keystroke) [input](#part0003_split_082.html_input) and to create a custom options dialog.

Maze Generator can generate a [random](#part0003_split_082.html_random) maze of any size. It will generate either a maze or an [anti-maze](#part0003_split_082.html_anti-maze). The path through an an anti-maze can only cross walls and cannot move through open areas.

The object of the game is to move the green ball to the red ball by pressing cursor movement keys.

### Greedy

![](images/00010.jpeg)

Learn to use clickable, changeable drawings for the dice in this game. You'll also learn to arrange many kinds of content in one window.

The object of Greedy is to achieve the highest possible score in ten rounds. Roll the dice many times in a round for a higher score. But don't be too greedy; a bad roll could result in the loss of all the points for that round!

### Word Builder

![](images/00011.jpeg)

Learn to combine color, images, and text in clickable drawings, and to [resize](#part0003_split_082.html_resize) window contents.

The object of Word Builder is to build words using all the tiles on the board. Points are given for each letter used. The longer the word, the more each letter is worth.

This game comes complete with a dictionary of more than 168,000 words.

### Image Resizer

![](images/00012.jpeg)

Learn to add a [toolbar](#part0003_split_082.html_toolbar), to allow the program user to draw with the mouse, and to save image files.

Image Resizer can be used to resize and [crop](#part0003_split_082.html_crop) an image from a [JPEG](#part0003_split_082.html_JPEG) file to any size, while maintaining the image's original proportions.

### Baker's Dozen Solitaire

![](images/00013.jpeg)

Learn to create a new image file drawn entirely with Java, and to allow the program user to drag and drop items around the window using the mouse.

The object of Baker's Dozen Solitaire is to move four rows of thirteen cards to the four top foundation stacks. Only one card may be moved at a time. Each foundation stack must be started with an ace. Cards may be moved to the foundation stacks in increasing numerical order and must be of the same suit. Each foundation stack ends with a king. Cards of any suit may be moved to other columns, but they must be placed in decreasing numerical order.

## Do You Know Basic Java?

This book assumes you already know how to do the following basic Java programming tasks, taught in the first book of this series, *Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Computer Programming*. Instructions for how to do the tasks marked with an asterisk, *, are also included at the back of this book, in [*Appendix D - Using Eclipse*](#part0003_split_089.html_Appendix-D---Using-Eclipse).

*   *Create [Java projects](#part0003_split_082.html_Java-project), [packages](#part0003_split_082.html_package), and [classes](#part0003_split_082.html_class).
*   *Inherit from a [superclass](#part0003_split_082.html_superclass) ([extend](#part0003_split_082.html_extend) another class).
*   *Add projects to the [build path](#part0003_split_082.html_build-path).
*   Create a [*main()* method](#part0003_split_082.html_main()-method) and one or more [constructors](#part0003_split_082.html_constructor).
*   *Save, [run](#part0003_split_082.html_run), and [export](#part0003_split_082.html_export) a program into an executable [JAR file](#part0003_split_082.html_JAR-file).
*   [Import](#part0003_split_082.html_import) other classes.
*   Create and use [variables](#part0003_split_082.html_variable): [String](#part0003_split_082.html_string), [int](#part0003_split_082.html_int), [double](#part0003_split_082.html_double), [char](#part0003_split_082.html_character), and [boolean](#part0003_split_082.html_boolean).
*   Create and use [instance variables](#part0003_split_082.html_instance-variable): [private](#part0003_split_082.html_private), [public](#part0003_split_082.html_public), [protected](#part0003_split_082.html_protected), [static](#part0003_split_082.html_static), and/or [final](#part0003_split_082.html_final).
*   Create and use [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method): private, public, protected, static, with or without [parameters](#part0003_split_082.html_parameter), and with or without a [return](#part0003_split_082.html_return) value.
*   Use [if/else](#part0003_split_082.html_if-statement) statements and [switch statements](#part0003_split_082.html_switch-statement).
*   Use [*while* loops](#part0003_split_082.html_while-loop) and [*for* loops](#part0003_split_082.html_for-loop).
*   Use the [not operator](#part0003_split_082.html_not-operator), [logical and operator](#part0003_split_082.html_logical-and-operator), and [logical or operator](#part0003_split_082.html_logical-or-operator).
*   Add, subtract, multiply, and divide numbers.
*   Change the order of operation using parentheses.
*   [Convert](#part0003_split_082.html_convert) a string value to an [integer](#part0003_split_082.html_integer) value.
*   Convert an integer or [character](#part0003_split_082.html_character) value to a string value.
*   Use [try/catch blocks](#part0003_split_082.html_try/catch-block) to handle one or more [exceptions](#part0003_split_082.html_exception).
*   Use different string methods.
*   Use the Random class to generate a random number.
*   Add [comments](#part0003_split_082.html_comment).
*   Print to the output [console](#part0003_split_082.html_console).
*   Use [arrays](#part0003_split_082.html_array) and [ArrayLists](#part0003_split_082.html_ArrayList).
*   Read from and write to a file.
*   End a program using System's exit() method.
*   Locate and fix [syntax errors](#part0003_split_082.html_syntax-error) and [run time errors](#part0003_split_082.html_run-time-error).

# Project 1 - Wizard of Yes/No

Do you ever have trouble making a decision? If you have a simple question requiring a yes or no answer, Wizard of Yes/No can suggest an answer.

This project will give you a quick introduction to the basics of creating windows with text.

Here is a screenshot of the Wizard of Yes/No program:

![](images/00014.jpeg)

## Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window

You'll first have to create a window if you want to work with graphics and [events](#part0003_split_082.html_event).

### Try It - Create a Window

Start writing the Wizard of Yes/No program by following the steps in this list.

1.  Create a new *Java project* called *Wizard of Yes No*. (Hint: the minimum JRE required for the programs in this book is Java SE 1.7\. When you create the project, select the execution environment JRE of *JavaSE-1.7* or higher.)
2.  Create a new *package* called *___________._____________.wizardofyesno* in the project. (Hint: as explained in the first book, the package name should be unique to you, all lower case, no spaces, and names separated by periods. Most businesses use their company name. You could use your first and last name. I'll use annette.godtland throughout these examples.)
3.  Create a new *class* called *WizardOfYesNo,* with superclass [*JFrame*](#part0003_split_082.html_JFrame) and with a [stub](#part0003_split_082.html_stub) for *main()*. (Hint: the only modifier needed is *public*. Do not select the *Create the constructors from superclass* option, nor the *Inherit abstract methods* option.)

Eclipse will create code for the *WizardOfYesNo* class that looks like the listing below.

### Run It

Throughout the lessons, unless there are [syntax errors](#part0003_split_082.html_syntax-error), save changes and run the program after every code change.

What happened?

### Key Points and More

*   Use *JFrame* as the *superclass* for programs that start with a window.
*   Create a new [instance](#part0003_split_082.html_instance) of the class in the *main()* method.
*   Create a constructor with no parameters.
*   In the constructor, use JFrame's *setVisible()* method to make the window visible:

```
setVisible(true)
```

*   *   Use *true* to make the window visible and *false* to hide it.
    *   *setVisible()* isn't actually [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define) in the JFrame class. It is defined in the Window class that JFrame extends. Because JFrame extends Window and *setVisible()* is a public method in Window, JFrame may use *setVisible()* as JFrame's own method. Therefore, for simplicity's sake, this book will refer to a class's inherited methods and variables as the class's own methods and variables.
*   In the constructor, use JFrame's *setDefaultCloseOperation()* method, with JFrame's *EXIT_ON_CLOSE* variable, to end the program when the window is closed.

```
setDefaultCloseOperation(EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
```

*   Several choices exist for the close operation:
    *   EXIT_ON_CLOSE - close the window and exit the program. This is the option used for all the programs in this book.
    *   DISPOSE_ON_CLOSE - close the window and any other windows used by this program before exiting the program.
    *   DO_NOTHING_ON_CLOSE - do nothing. You would use this option if you wanted to write additional code that should run when the window is closed.
    *   HIDE_ON_CLOSE - keep the program running but make the window no longer visible when the window is closed.
*   If a [default](#part0003_split_082.html_default) close operation is not set, closing the window makes the window invisible but the program keeps running.

Java uses a default font if the named font isn't on the computer. The default font could make things fit differently than you expected. So what font should you use if don't know what fonts might be available on the computer on which the program might run?

1.  Try each of the font family names for the name of the font for *font*. (Hint: change Font's first parameter value, Font's *name*. Use Font's *DIALOG*, *DIALOG_INPUT*, *SANS_SERIF*, *SERIF*, or *MONOSPACED* variable.)

### Key Points and More

*   Create a new Font object by calling Font's constructor with three parameter values:
    *   Font - name a font in quotes, or name one of the five font family static variables: *DIALOG*, *DIALOG_INPUT*, *SANS_SERIF*, *SERIF*, or *MONOSPACED*. Use “Font.” in front of the font family names, because they are static variables.
    *   Style - name one of three style static variables: *PLAIN, BOLD*, or *ITALIC*. You may add *BOLD* and *ITALIC* together to select a bold and italic font style. Use “Font.” in front of the style names, because they are static variables.
    *   Size - use an integer for the size of the font.
*   A named font must exist on the computer on which the program is run. Otherwise the program will use a default font.
*   If you name a font family, Java will look for a font on the computer from that font family.
*   If you use a font too large to fit in the window, the text will be displayed as an ellipse, ….
*   Set the font of a label using JLabel's *setFont()* method, with a font as the parameter value.
*   Fonts can be applied to other components that display text. You will add fonts to other components in later lessons.

## Lesson 1.8 - Serial Version UID

In this lesson you'll learn to stop Eclipse from showing the warning message about serialization.

### Try It - Prevent the Serial Version UID Warning

A warning in Eclipse says:

```
The serializable class WizardOfYesNo does not declare a static final serialVersionUID of type long
```

Use Quick Fix to easily fix the [serial version UID](#part0003_split_082.html_serial-version-UID) warning.

1.  Use Quick Fix to *Add default serial version ID*:
    1.  Rest your mouse on the word marked as a warning: *WizardOfYesNo*.
    2.  After a moment, Quick Fix options appear. Choose the option to add the default serial version ID.
2.  Remove the extra comments and blank lines that Quick Fix added.

*Listing 1-23, from WizardOfYesNo.java*

* * *

```
 ...

public class WizardOfYesNo extends JFrame {
  private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
  private static final String[] ANSWER =  
    {"Yes",

      ...
```

* * *

*[Completed listing](#part0003_split_083.html_cl1-23)*

The private static final [long](#part0003_split_082.html_long) instance variable called *serialVersionUID* should be added to your code, set to value 1L, and the warning in Eclipse should now be gone.

### Run It

Running the program should produce the same results as before.

### Key Points and More

*   Some warnings can be safely ignored. However, fix problems that cause warnings if you can.
*   Use Quick Fix to easily fix problems like the missing serial version UID. To use Quick Fix, rest your mouse on the word marked as causing the error, then choose a fix from the list. The code will automatically be changed, according to the fix you chose.
*   Java expects JFrames and many other components to have a *serialVersionUID*. The ID is meant to be unique for the current version of the class. The ID would be needed if you ever serialize the class. However, you won't serialize any of the classes in this book and explaining serialization is beyond the scope of this book. So you may ignore this warning.
*   However, because you're asked to create a *serialVersionUID* anyway, you could use the *serialVersionUID* as a way to label the version of the program. Use any integer value. The “L” after the integer means the integer is a long integer. You can set this first version of this program to 1L. If you create a new version of this program later, you could change the version number to 2L. Think of 1L and 2L values as version 1.0 and version 2.0.

## Lesson 1.9 - Event Queue

Did you notice the import statement that Eclipse inserted for JFrame? The import statement shows JFrame is in the javax.swing package. Therefore, JFrame is a Swing component. Java expects all Swing objects to be created on an [event queue](#part0003_split_082.html_event-queue).

### Try It - Create WizardOfYesNo on the EventQueue

1.  Replace the code in the *main()* method with code exactly as shown. (Hint: to make this lengthy, oddly [formatted](#part0003_split_082.html_format) code easier to type, use Ctrl-Space. Eclipse will then insert all the necessary imports, formatting and punctuation. Hint: if you type the code without using Ctrl-Space for help, import EventQueue from java.awt.)
    1.  Type “Event” and press Ctrl-Space for help. Choose *EventQueue*.
    2.  Type “.in” and press Ctrl-Space for help. Choose *invokeLater()*.
    3.  Type “new Run” in the parentheses and press Ctrl-Space for help. Choose *Runnable*. Eclipse will insert “Runnable” as well as the outline for the *run()* method.
    4.  Type “new WizardOfYesNo();” in the *run()* method.
    5.  Remove the comments and extra blank lines that Eclipse inserted.

*Listing 1-24, from WizardOfYesNo.java*

* * *

```
 ...

  public static void main(String[] args) {
    EventQueue.invokeLater(new Runnable() {
      public void run() {
        new WizardOfYesNo();
      }
    });
  }
    ...
```

* * *

*[Completed listing](#part0003_split_083.html_cl1-24)*

### Run It

The program should still run with the same results, but may now run faster.

### Key Points and More

*   This program may have been running fine without creating WizardOfYesNo on an event queue. However, sometimes program code may not run in the expected order if the swing objects aren't created on the event queue.
*   *main()* does not run on the event queue. Therefore, write code to add the creation of any swing objects created in *main()* to the event queue. For example, if MyGame extends JFrame, add the creation of the MyGame object to the event queue in *main()* like this:

```
public static void main(String[] args) {
	EventQueue.invokeLater(new Runnable() {
		public void run() {
			new MyGame();
		}
	});
}
```

*   All objects created by any object created on the event queue will automatically be created on the event queue as well. So for all the programs in this book, only the swing objects created in *main()* require code to add the object to the event queue.
*   “invokeLater”, “Runnable”, and “run()” are all related to Java threads. Threads are not covered in this book. Threads will be covered in the next book, *Advanced Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Threads and Animated Video Games*. For now, just know that you should create the instance of your program in *main()* by placing a call to your program's constructor on the event queue.
*   Ctrl-Space brings up options for Eclipse to complete code for you.
*   To easily enter the code that will call other code from an event queue, do the following: (Hint: Eclipse will then insert all the necessary imports, formatting and punctuation.)
    *   Type “Event” and press Ctrl-Space for help. Choose *EventQueue*.
    *   Type “.in” and press Ctrl-Space for help. Choose *invokeLater()*.
    *   Type “new Run” in the parentheses and press Ctrl-Space for help. Choose *Runnable*. Eclipse will insert Runnable as well as the outline for the *run()* method.
    *   Call the other code in the *run()* method.
    *   Remove the comments and extra blank lines that Eclipse inserted.

## Lesson 1.10 - Cross Platform Look and Feel

Windows, dialogs, and the components they contain, look different on computers with different [operating systems](#part0003_split_082.html_operating-system). This difference affects how code should be written. In order to get program code in this book to work the same, regardless what operating system you are running on, use the Cross Platform [look and feel](#part0003_split_082.html_look-and-feel).

### Key Points and More

*   Java is designed so programs you create can run on computers with many different operating systems. Each operating system looks different. Windows components look different than OS X components and they both look different than Linux components. These differences are called the look and feel of the components.
*   Java came up with its own look and feel, a metallic look and feel, meant to be used as a cross platform look and feel. If you use this look and feel, your program will look the same on every computer, whether the program is run on Windows, OS X, Linux, or anything else. To use the same look and feel on every computer, use:

```
try {
	String className = UIManager.getCrossPlatformLookAndFeelClassName();
	UIManager.setLookAndFeel(className);
}
catch (Exception e) {}
```

*   If you use the system look and feel, the program will look more like other programs being run on that particular operating system, whether it be Windows, OS X, or Linux. To make your program look like other programs running on that computer, use:

```
try {
	String className = UIManager.getSystemLookAndFeelClassName();
	UIManager.setLookAndFeel(className);
}
catch (Exception e) {}
```

*   You should decide which is more important to you: having your program look the same on every operating system or having your program match the look and feel of each operating system. If your program looks the same on every operating system, you will know everyone will see the program exactly the way you do, but the program user may not be as comfortable using the program. If the program matches the look and feel of each operating system, the user may be more comfortable using the program, but the resulting layout or components could sometimes look bad without your knowledge.
*   Some of the programs in this book use colored buttons. Setting colors on buttons when using either the Windows look and feel or the OS X look and feel does not have the desired effect. Therefore, these programs should use the cross platform look and feel.

# Project 2 - Guess My Color

The Guess My Color game shows a sample color, initially black, and a target color. The object of the game is to slowly add or remove small amounts of red, green, and blue from the sample to try to match the target color.

Even if you don't see color differences well, consider writing this game anyway. Guess My Color is a good introduction for how to work with colors, panels, layouts, buttons, and message dialogs.

Here is a screenshot of the Guess My Color program:

![](images/00004.jpeg)

### Key Points and More

*   A JFrame window uses a border layout for arranging components in a window. The border layout's class name is BorderLayout.
*   Each of BorderLayout's five areas can hold only one component.
    *   The top area is referred to as page start.
    *   The bottom area is referred to as page end.
    *   The left area is referred to as line start.
    *   The right area is referred to as line end.
    *   The large middle area is referred to as center.
*   Always set a location whenever you add a component to a BorderLayout. The BorderLayout's location variables are *PAGE_START*, *PAGE_END*, *LINE_START*, *LINE_END*, and *CENTER*. These variables are static variables, so use “BorderLayout.” with these variables. For example, to add a JLabel called *nameLabel* to the top of a window, use:

```
add(nameLabel, BorderLayout.PAGE_START);
```

*   If a component is added to a BorderLayout without setting a location, the program puts the component in the center area.
*   If a second component is located in an area of a BorderLayout that already has a component, the second component will replace the first component.
*   Components added to the areas of a BorderLayout will be stretched to fill the window:
    *   Components added to the top and bottom areas will be stretched as wide as the window.
    *   Components added to the side areas will be stretched in height as tall as the middle area.
    *   Components added to the middle area will be stretched in height to the same height as the side areas, and stretched in width to make the total side and middle areas as wide as the window.
    *   You should see these five areas as colored rectangles in the next lesson.
*   If nothing is added to an area of a BorderLayout, that area will not be included in the window.
*   *LINE_START* and *LINE_END* are relative locations. If the component's orientation is *LEFT_TO_RIGHT, LINE_START* refers to the left area and *LINE_END* refers to the right area. If the component's orientation is *RIGHT_TO_LEFT, LINE_START* refers to the right area and *LINE_END* refers to the left area. Component's default orientation is *LEFT_TO_RIGHT.* To change a component's orientation, use Component's *setComponentOriention()* method.
*   BorderLayout's five areas may also be referred to as *NORTH*, *SOUTH*, *EAST*, *WEST*, and *CENTER*. *NORTH* is the same as *PAGE_START*. *SOUTH* is the same as *PAGE_END*. *EAST* is always to the right of *CENTER*. And *WEST* is always to the left of *CENTER*. However, Java standards recommend that you use *PAGE_START*, *PAGE_END*, *LINE_START*, and *LINE_END* so your program may more easily be adapted for languages that have different orientations.

### Try It - Set the Panel Preferred Size

Setting the panel size was an unfair task. When you ran GuessMyColor again, the black and cyan panels were still small. Why were they still small? Because you packed the window after you set the panel's size. *pack()* ignores the size set for a component. Instead, *pack()* checks for the component's preferred size.

Setting a preferred size requires a Dimension. A Dimension is made up of integers for width and height.

1.  Before setting the background color of *samplePanel*, create a new Dimension object called *size* that is 50 [pixels](#part0003_split_082.html_pixel) wide and 50 pixels high.

### Key Points and More

*   Organize window contents by placing them in panels.
*   The default layout for a JFrame is BorderLayout. The default layout for a JPanel is [FlowLayout](#part0003_split_082.html_FlowLayout). The layout used for a JFrame or JPanel can be changed. Later lessons will show you how to change the layout and will introduce you to other layouts.
*   If more than one component is placed in a panel using FlowLayout, the components will appear side by side, centered in the panel, in the order they were added.
*   JPanels can be placed inside other JPanels.
*   To add to a container that uses FlowLayout, only the component need be given for the *add()* method, without giving a location. For example, to add a JLabel called *nameLabel* to a JPanel called *centerPanel*, use:

```
centerPanel.add(nameLabel);
```

*   *pack()* will reduce a window and all of its contents to their preferred sizes. If a component packs smaller than you want it, set the component's preferred size using its *setPreferredSize()* method.
*   A dimension is made up of two integers: width and height.
*   To set the preferred size of a component, create a new dimension with the preferred width and height, then set the preferred size using that dimension. For example, to set the preferred size of a JLabel called *titleLabel* to 100 pixels wide by 50 pixels high, use:

```
Dimension size = new Dimension(100, 50);
titleLabel.setPreferredSize(size);
```

*   In some layouts, if 0 is used for either the width or height of the preferred size, the layout will use any value for that dimension. For example, to set a *titleLabel* height of 50 pixels, with whatever width fits best in the window, create *size* like this:

```
Dimension size = new Dimension(0, 50);
```

## Lesson 2.5 - Opacity

Components may be either [opaque](#part0003_split_082.html_opaque) or [transparent](#part0003_split_082.html_transparent). Opaque components cover up components positioned behind them, but transparent components allow underlying components to be seen. A component can be changed from opaque to transparent, or from transparent to opaque.

### Try It - Make a Label Opaque

Why is the color of *titleLabel* still gray? A JLabel is transparent, so its own background color cannot be seen. Instead, the background color of the container behind a JLabel is seen. To see the background color of a JLabel, make the label opaque.

1.  Set *titleLabel* to opaque. (Hint: use JLabel's *setOpaque()* method.)

*Listing 2-13, from GuessMyColor.java*

* * *

```
 ...

  private void initGUI() {

      ...

    titleLabel.setBackground(Color.BLACK);
    titleLabel.setForeground(Color.WHITE);
    titleLabel.setOpaque(_________);
    add(titleLabel, BorderLayout.PAGE_START);

      ...
```

* * *

*[Completed listing](#part0003_split_083.html_cl2-13)*

### Run It

The top panel should now display a black background.

### Key Points and More

*   An opaque component is solid, not transparent. In other words, an opaque component covers up any object displayed behind it.
*   A component that is not opaque is transparent. In other words, a transparent component allows underlying components to be seen.
*   A transparent component's text is visible, if that text is a different color than the background color of the container behind the component.
*   Most components are opaque by default. JLabels, however, are transparent by default.
*   Any component can be made opaque or transparent by using the component's *setOpaque()* method. Use *true* to make the component opaque. Use *false* to make the component transparent.
*   A component's background color is only visible if the component is opaque.

### Key Points and More

*   Buttons are components that, when clicked, cause an event for which the program can perform an action.
*   Create a button by creating a new JButton object with the button's text as a parameter value. For example, to create a button called *okButton* with text “OK”, use:

```
JButton okButton = new JButton("OK");
```

*   Set the color of a button with JButton's *setBackground()* method.
    *   To set the color of a button when using the cross platform look and feel, simply set the background color. For example, to make the above *okButton* green, use:

```
okButton.setBackground(Color.GREEN);
```

*   *   To set the color of a button when using OS X look and feel, set the background color, make the button opaque and do not paint the border. For example, to make the above *okButton* green, use:

```
okButton.setBackground(Color.GREEN);
okButton.setOpaque(true);
okButton.setBorderPainted(false);
```

*   *   To set the color of a button when using Windows look and feel, set the background color, set the content area to be filled, and make the button opaque. Note, you must make the button opaque after setting the content area to be filled because setting the content area to be filled also sets opaque to false. For example, to make the above *okButton* green, use:

```
okButton.setBackground(Color.GREEN);
okButton.setContetAreaFilled(true);
okButton.setOpaque(true);
```

*   *   Note, there is no way to create a colored button with a border for either the OS X look and feel or the Windows look and feel. The next few games in this book require borders around the buttons, so the games must be created using the cross platform look and feel.
*   Set the font of the text on a button with JButton's *setFont()* method.
*   A later lesson will show you how to create a button with an image instead of text.
*   Program a button to perform an action by adding an action listener to the button. Add an action listener using JButton's *addActionListener()* method, with a new ActionListener as the parameter value.
    *   The action listener requires a method called *actionPerformed()*, with one parameter, an [ActionEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_ActionEvent), and returns nothing.
    *   The *actionPerformed()* method usually calls a private method in the same class to perform the desired task.
*   For example, to add an action listener to a JButton called *okButton* that will call *doIt()* when the button is clicked, use:

```
okButton.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
	public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
		doIt();
	}
});
```

*   To easily enter this lengthy, oddly formatted code:
    *   Type “okButton.add” and press Ctrl-Space. Select addActionListener.
    *   Inside the parentheses, type “new Act” and press Ctrl-Space. Select ActionListener.
    *   Add the line of code “doIt();” in the *actionPerformed()* method.
    *   Remove any comments you don't want.

## Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs

A [message dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_message-dialog) is a small window that displays a message.

### Try It - Display a Message Dialog

What should GuessMyColor do if the sample color matches the target color? Open a small window to congratulate the user.

1.  In *updateColorSample(),* check whether each color matches its target color. (Hint: add System.out.println statements if you want to see the color values and target color values as you test GuessMyColor. Be sure to remove all System.out.println statements later.)
2.  If all three colors match:
    1.  Create a string called *message* to congratulate the user and tell him the color values.
    2.  Display *message* in a message dialog. (Hint: use [JOptionPane's](#part0003_split_082.html_JOptionPane) *showMessageDialog()* method, with *this* and *message* as parameter values.)

### Key Points and More

*   The easiest way to display a message to the user is to call JOptionPane's *showMessageDialog()* method. Use *this* as the first parameter value and the message as the second parameter value. *showMessageDialog()* is a static method, so use the class name to call the method. For example, to display “Hello World!” in a message box, use:

```
JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this, "Hello World!");
```

*   Use *this* as the first parameter value, to center the message dialog over the component that called the method.
*   Use [*null*](#part0003_split_082.html_null) as the first parameter value, to center the message in the middle of the screen.
*   The first parameter value must be a type of component or *null*. If the class that's displaying the message doesn't extend a component, you'll have to use *null* for the first parameter value.

*   The added *My Components* project will be included in the exported JAR file as long as your project was exported as instructed in [*Appendix D - Using Eclipse*](#part0003_split_089.html_Appendix-D---Using-Eclipse).

### Key Points and More

*   Use a JTextArea for displaying multiple lines of text.
*   To wrap text across lines, turn line wrap on with JTextArea's *setLineWrap()* method. If you want the lines to wrap at word boundaries, turn on word wrap style too, with JTextArea's *setWrapStyleWord()* method.
*   A JTextArea component is often used to take input from the program user. So JTextArea's default settings allow the user to edit the component's text. If you only want to display text in the text area, disable editing with JTextArea's *setEditable()* method.

# Project 4 - Framed

This next project is the Framed game. Framed will create a 3x3 grid of lights, some on (red) and others off (black). Clicking lights will [toggle](#part0003_split_082.html_toggle) the on/off state of a groups of lights:

*   Click a corner light to toggle the four lights in that corner.
*   Click a middle side light to toggle all the lights on that side.
*   Click the center light to toggle it and the lights directly above, below, and to each side of it.

The goal is to turn on all but the center light, thus forming a frame.

Here is a screenshot of the Framed program after the game has been solved:

![](images/00005.jpeg)

Keep all of a class's capabilities and add more, by extending the class. To create a custom button like a light button, extend JButton.

This lesson will also demonstrate conditions requiring use of *this* to identify instance variables.

### Key Points and More

*   Extend the JButton class to create a clickable object with capabilities similar to a JButton.
*   A class extended from the JButton class can use JButton's public or protected methods, such as JButton's *setBackground()*, *getBackground()*, and *setPreferredSize()* methods.
*   By extending the class, additional information can be kept with a button, such as row and column. The extended class can also provide additional methods, like *turnOn(),* *turnOff()*, and *isLit()*.
*   Java Programmers often give a method's parameter variables the same names as the instance variables for which each of the parameters provides a value. Doing so makes it easier to remember the purpose of the method's parameters. Plus, Eclipse displays the parameters' names when it shows instant help for the method. Therefore, method parameter variable names should be clear, descriptive names. Because the best variable name is likely already used for the instance variable name, it is often easier to use the same name for the method's parameter variable than to invent another good name.
*   If an instance variable has the same name as a variable [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) in a method or as a method parameter, refer to an instance variable *name* as *this.name*.
*   For example, if a class MyGame has an integer instance variable called *points,* and MyGame's constructor takes an integer parameter called *points* whose value should be put in the points instance variable, use:

```
private int points;
public MyGame(int points) {
	this.points = points;
}
```

### Key Points and More

*   The numbers of rows and columns must be provided when a new GridLayout object is created. A 0 for either value fills that row or column with whatever number fits in the container.
*   Components will be added to one column of the GridLayout until that column is full. Then components will be added to the next column until it is full, and so on. Basically, the value for column is ignored unless the value for rows is 0
*   All components added to a GridLayout must have the same size. If they do not, smaller components will be stretched to match the size of the largest component.

### Key Points and More

*   To create a new ActionListener, an *actionPerformed()* method must be provided, with one parameter, an ActionEvent. The *actionPerformed()* method can use any of ActionEvent's methods on the ActionEvent variable.
*   One often-used ActionEvent method is *getSource()*. It will get the object that caused the event. However, the *getSource()* method returns an object of type Object.
*   Every Java class a programmer creates actually extends the Object class as its base class. But Java can't call the methods that were added when the class was extended if the object's instance has only type Object. A programmer must tell Java that the object is also a type of the created class. In other words, the object must be cast to the created class. Casting is done by putting the name of the class to which the object is being cast, in parentheses before the object reference (variable name) that must be cast. For example, to cast a variable called *result* to a type called Card and assign *result* to a Card object called *myCard*, use:

```
Card myCard = (Card)result;
```

*   A run time error occurs if a program tries to cast an object to a type and the object is not of that type. For example, a run time error would occur if the program tried to cast the above *result* to a type called Car.
*   Later lessons will demonstrate more common methods used for events handled by other [listeners](#part0003_split_082.html_listener).

### Key Points and More

*   The easiest way to ask a program user a yes/no question is to display the question in a confirm dialog, using JOptionPane's *showConfirmDialog()* method.
*   The first two parameters of *showConfirmDialog()* are the same as *showMessageDialog()*: *this* and the string message. The third parameter is the string title for the window, and the fourth parameter is the option type.
*   The option type parameter controls which options to give the user. All the confirm dialogs in this book use JOptionPane's YES_NO_OPTION variable, so the user has only two options: yes or no.
*   The confirm dialog returns an integer. That integer is equal to JOptionPane's *YES_OPTION* if the user clicked *Yes* and equal to JOptionPane's *NO_OPTION* if he clicked *No*.
*   For example, to ask a user if he wants to start over, then check whether he clicked *Yes*, use:

```
int option = JOptionPane.showConfirmDialog(this, "Do you want to start over?", "Start Over?", JOptionPane.YES_NO_OPTION);
if (option == JOptionPane.YES_OPTION) {
```

# Project 5 - Watch Your Step

Next you'll create the Watch Your Step game. The Watch Your Step game consists of a grid of tiles in 10 rows and 10 columns. Hidden behind ten of the tiles are black holes. Hidden behind some of the other tiles is the number of black holes in neighboring tiles. Click a tile to reveal what is behind it. If that tile has no number, the game will also reveal that tile's neighbors. The goal is to reveal all the tiles without clicking on a black hole.

Here is a screenshot of the Watch Your Step program in the middle of a game:

![](images/00006.jpeg)

### Key Points and More

*   While a button is in focus, pressing the space bar will cause an action event on that button. In other words, pressing the space bar will make a program behave as though the user clicked the button.
*   Pressing the tab key will move the focus from one button to the next.
*   Normally, whenever a button is in focus, a box is drawn around the button's text. The box is a visual indicator so the program user can readily see which button is in focus.
*   You can make a button not show the focus indicator by using JButton's *setFocusPainted()* method, with *false* as its parameter value.
*   Turning off the focus indicator simply stops the program from drawing a box around the button's text. Pressing the space bar will still cause an action event on that button and pressing the tab key will still move the focus from one button to the next.
*   Space bar activation and tab focus movement are capabilities that come with a JButton. Turning off those capabilities is beyond the scope of this book. If you don't want those capabilities active, you might be better off creating clickable components without extending JButton, as will be demonstrated in later lessons.

# Project 6 - Sliding Tiles

Next you'll create the Sliding Tiles game. A photo will be divided into 16 tiles in 4 rows and 4 columns, with the bottom right corner missing. The tiles will then be [scrambled](#part0003_split_082.html_scramble) and you will be challenged to slide the tiles back into their original positions. Once all the tiles are in the correct order, the missing tile from the bottom right corner will also be displayed.

To slide a tile, you must click a tile next to the empty space. Doing so will slide the clicked tile into that empty space.

Here is a screenshot of the Sliding Tiles program:

![](images/00007.jpeg)

### Key Points and More

*   Use ImageIO's *read()* method to read an image file. *read()* returns a BufferedImage object.
*   ImageIO's *read()* method is a static method of ImageIO. So use “ImageIO.” in front of *read()* to call *read().*
*   ImageIO's *read()* method needs a File parameter value. You can create a new File object using the file's name. So to read a file named “smile.gif” and put it in a BufferedImage called *image*, use:

```
image = ImageIO.read(new File("smile.gif"));
```

*   If you do not provide a path as part of the file name, like in the above example:
    *   The file must be placed in your project's *bin* folder of your Java work folder, in order to run your program in Eclipse.
    *   The file must be placed in the same folder as the generated JAR file, in order to run your program outside of Eclipse.
*   ImageIO's *read()* method will throw an IOException if an error occurred while reading the file, and an IllegalArgumentException if the File parameter value is *null*.
*   BufferedImage's *getSubimage()* method retrieves a rectangular piece of an image. Give *getSubimage()* the x and y coordinates of the upper left corner of the piece wanted along with its width and height. For example, to get a piece of an image called *image*, starting 10 pixels from the left edge, 20 pixels from the top, 320 pixels wide and 240 pixels tall, use:

```
image.getSubimage(10, 20, 320, 240);
```

*   BufferedImage's *getSubimage()* method will return a BufferedImage object.
*   BufferedImage's *getSubimage()* method will throw a RasterFormatException if the method's parameter values do not refer to an area within the image.
*   The ImageIcon constructor can create a new ImageIcon object from an [Image](#part0003_split_082.html_Image) object, a BufferedImage object, or a string that gives the path and name of an image file.
    *   For example, to create an ImageIcon object called *myIcon* from a file called “smile.gif”, use:

```
ImageIcon myIcon = new ImageIcon("smile.gif");
```

*   *   For example, to create an ImageIcon object called *myIcon* from a BufferedImage object called *smileImage*, use:

```
ImageIcon myIcon = new ImageIcon(smileImage);
```

*   An ImageIcon is not a type of Image, so an ImageIcon may not be used where Images are expected, nor may an Image be used where an ImageIcon is expected.
*   An ImageIcon object provides fewer methods and less information than an Image object.

[Project 7 - Maze Generator and Anti-Maze](#part0003_split_040.html_Project-7---Maze-Generator-and-Anti-Maze) will introduce concepts that you should understand before trying Project 8.

### Key Points and More

*   You can remove a component from a panel by calling JPanel's *remove()* method with the component to be removed.
*   You can remove all components from a panel by calling JPanel's *removeAll()* method.
*   If you add or remove components from a panel after the panel has been displayed, you must redisplay the panel by calling JPanel's *revalidate()* method. This will force the program to [repaint](#part0003_split_082.html_repaint) all of the components currently in the panel and recalculate the panel's layout if necessary.

# Project 7 - Maze Generator and Anti-Maze

Next you'll create a Maze Generator game, which will generate a random maze. Maze Generator will respond to cursor movement keys to move a ball from the top left corner of the maze to the bottom right corner.

Here is a screenshot of the Maze Generator program:

![](images/00008.jpeg)

Anti-Maze is Maze Generator with a slight change: you may only move through the maze by crossing a line. You cannot cross open space.

Here is a screenshot of the Anti-Maze program:

![](images/00009.jpeg)

### Try It - Draw a Rectangle on a Panel

Drawing a rectangle is similar to drawing a line: use *drawRect()* with the location of the top left corner of the rectangle and the width and height of the rectangle. To draw a rectangle at 0, 5, 10 pixels wide, and 20 pixels tall, use:

```
g.drawRect(0, 5, 10, 20)
```

In what color would the rectangle be drawn? The default is black. But if you want to use a different color, first switch the color with Graphics' *setColor()* method.

You can also draw a filled rectangle using a method similar to *drawRect()*:

```
g.fillRect(0, 5, 10, 20)
```

How do you generate a maze with only one way to reach any cell and with no unreachable cells?

*   Start at a random cell.
*   While not all cells have yet been visited,
    *   Find all neighbors with all walls intact.
    *   If one or more was found:
        *   If more than one was found, add that cell to the list to try later.
        *   Pick a neighbor and remove the adjacent wall.
        *   Go to the neighbor and increment the number visited.
    *   If none was found, go to one of the cells saved in the list to try later.

Adding comments for planned code helps you plan the steps and organize your code.

### Key Points and More

*   To draw on a JPanel, create a public method for that panel called *paintComponent()*. *paintComponent()* should take one parameter, a Graphics object, and return nothing.
*   Java will call *paintComponent()* any time your window is moved, [minimized](#part0003_split_082.html_minimized), [maximized](#part0003_split_082.html_maximized), hidden behind another window, or when your program tells the window to repaint. So *paintComponent()* must redraw the entire panel whenever *paintComponent()* is called.
*   Graphics has many drawing and painting methods. The ones used in this lesson and used again in many others include:
    *   *setColor()* - sets the current drawing color. *setColor()* requires a Color parameter. The parameter value may be any of the predefined colors or a new Color object.
    *   *drawLine()* - draws a line with the current drawing color. *drawLine()* requires four integer parameters: the x and y coordinates of where to start the line, and the x and y coordinates of where to end the line.
    *   *drawRect()* and *fillRect()* - draws the outline of a rectangle and a filled rectangle with the current drawing color. Each requires four parameters, giving the x and y coordinates of a corner of the rectangle, and the width and height of the rectangle.
    *   *drawOval()* and *fillOval()* - draws the outline of an oval and a filled oval with the current drawing color. Each requires four integer parameters. Imagine the rectangle that would contain the desired oval. Then give the x and y coordinates of a corner of that rectangle, and the width and height of that rectangle. To make a circle, use the same value for width and height.
    *   *drawString()* will be explained in a later lesson.
*   Try to keep the amount of work the *paintComponent()* method does to a minimum. You should try to make the *paintComponent()* code run as fast as possible.
*   Call JPanel's *repaint()* method whenever you want the panel painted again, such as when instance variables are changed that affect how the panel is painted.
*   Java calls *paintComponent()* whenever the window must be repainted for any reason.
*   Always call JPanel's *repaint()* method instead of its *paintComponent()* method. If you use *repaint()*, Java combines your request to paint the component with any other requests to paint the component into one paint process. For example, if the program user covers part of your program window with a different window, Windows will send another request to your program to repaint the component.
*   What is the difference between *repaint()* and *revalidate()*? *repaint()* redraws the component. *revalidate()* recalculates the layout of the component and any of the component's contained components. Call *repaint()* whenever the component's contents should be redrawn. Call *revalidate()* whenever the component may have changed size. Sometimes you may have to call both *revalidate()* and *repaint()*.
*   If you have a custom painted panel, you should also provide a public method called *getPreferredSize()*. *getPreferredSize()* should take no parameters and return a Dimension. The dimension should be the preferred size of the panel.
    *   Layout managers look for a *getPreferredSize()* method to figure out how much room to allow for the panel when packing the window. If no *getPreferredSize()* method is provided, the layout manager may not reserve any room for the panel.
    *   Why provide a *getPreferredSize()* method instead of using *setPreferredSize()* like you did in previous programs? You don't want the size of the panel to ever change, because you're drawing lines, rectangles, and circles a specific size on the panel. *setPreferredSize()* has no effect on a panel that has a *getPreferredSize()* method. By providing a *getPreferredSize()* method, you make sure the panel will always be displayed at that size and cannot be changed by a later call to *setPreferredSize()*.
*   When you create the Java Projects in this book, select the option to *Use an execution environment JRE of JavaSE-1.7* or higher. Once you select this option for creating a project, Eclipse will default to that option for all future Java Projects.

### Key Points and More

*   To make your program listen for keystrokes from the keyboard, add a key listener.
*   Instead of adding the key listener to a button, you'll add the key listener to the window itself (the JFrame).
*   To add a key listener to a window, use JFrame's *addKeyListener()* method.
*   To add a key listener, add a KeyAdapter object instead of a [KeyListener](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyListener) object. KeyAdapter extends KeyListener, so may be used anywhere KeyListener is allowed. But much less code is required for a KeyAdapter than for a KeyListener.
*   To make a KeyAdapter recognize when a key is pressed, add a public method to the KeyAdapter called *keyReleased()*. *keyReleased()* should have one parameter, a KeyEvent, and return nothing. For example, to add a key listener that calls *stop()* when any key is pressed, use:

```
addKeyListener(new KeyAdapter() {
	public void keyReleased(KeyEvent e) {
		stop();
	}
});
```

*   The KeyAdapter class comes with a *keyReleased()* method, but the method does nothing. By adding a *keyReleased()* method to your new KeyAdapter class, you're overriding the original method. However, the overriding method must be declared exactly the same as the *keyReleased()* method in the original KeyAdapter class. The overriding method must have the same name, visibility, type of parameter, and return type.
*   The KeyAdapter class also provides a *keyPressed()* method. Why did I have you use the *keyReleased()* method instead of *keyPressed()*? Usually, holding down a key on a keyboard signals repeated keyPressed events. Letting go of a key on the keyboard signals only one keyReleased event. If you want to make sure only one event is sent if the program user happens to hold down a key, use the *keyReleased()* method instead of the *keyPressed()* method.
*   Adapter classes are provided so you don't have to write as much code. If you had used the KeyListener class, you would have been required to provide code for the *keyPressed()*, *keyReleased()*, and *keyTyped()* methods. By using the KeyAdapter class, you could [override](#part0003_split_082.html_override) just those methods to which you want to add functionality. For that reason, for most listeners, you should probably create their adapters instead of directly creating the listener. However, not all listeners have corresponding adapters. The ActionListener class you've been using for JButtons does not have a corresponding ActionAdapter.
*   To get the character of the key that was pressed or released, use KeyEvent's *getKeyChar()* method and put the result in a character variable.
*   Some key strokes result in more than one key event, such as Shift-A or Ctrl-I.
*   Some key events, such as the shift key, alt key, cursor movement key, etc., don't have a character. So *getKeyChar()* doesn't get a valid character for those keys.
*   All key events have a key code. To get the key code for the key that was pressed or released, use KeyEvent's *getKeyCode()* method.
*   To see the possible key codes in Eclipse, type “KeyEvent.vk_” and press Ctrl-Space for Help.
*   The VK in the key code name stands for Virtual Key. For example, *VK_ENTER* is the code for the enter key.
*   For example, to get the key that was pressed, from KeyEvent *e,* and check whether that key was the enter key, use:

```
int keyCode = e.getKeyCode();
if (keyCode == KeyEvent.VK_ENTER) {
```

## Lesson 7.3 - Button Focus

While a component such as a button has focus, the component will respond to keyboard input. Buttons are created focusable by default. If a button is focusable, pressing the tab key will move focus between the button and other components in the panel. If the focus is on the button, pressing the space bar will activate the button.

However, if buttons in a window are focusable, any key listeners defined for that window will be ignored. In this lesson you will learn to make a button not focusable so the program will use the window's key listeners.

Or you can wait until [*Project 10 - Maze Generator Options Dialog*](#part0003_split_053.html_Project-10---Maze-Generator-Options-Dialog), when you'll add a dialog to allow the program user to set the the size of the maze and choose between a maze or an anti-maze.

### Key Points and More

*   The component listening for keyboard input is said to be the one in focus.
*   Only one component in a program can listen for keyboard input at a time.
*   Input fields listen for keyboard input so the user can type text in the field. Buttons listen for keyboard input so the user can use the space bar instead of the mouse to activate the button.
*   Normally, the user moves focus from one component to another by pressing the tab key.
*   KeyListeners only work while the component on which they are defined is in focus. Before you added the *New Maze* button to the Maze Generator, the JFrame was always in focus.
*   After you added the *New Maze* button, the button came into focus so the JFrame was no longer in focus.
*   Allowing the user to move focus between buttons and JPanels is fairly complex code and is beyond the scope of this book.
*   One easy solution to the problem of which component has focus is to remove the ability of buttons to take focus. You could then still click the button with the mouse to activate the button, but you would not be able to tab to the button or use the space bar to click the button. To remove the ability of a button to take focus, use JButton's *setFocusable()* method. Here's an example for a button called *nextButton.*

```
nextButton.setFocusable(false);
```

*   Another solution to the focus problem is to bring the window back into focus after adding the buttons. To do so, use JFrame's *requestFocusInWindow()* method. For example, to move focus to the window, use:

```
requestFocusInWindow();
```

*   Another solution would be to use key bindings instead of a KeyListener for the cursor movement keys. However, key bindings for JPanels are more complex to write than are key listeners, so key bindings are not covered in this book.

### Key Points and More

*   Menus are created as a group of menu objects: a menu bar, one or more menu on the menu bar, and zero or more menu items on each menu.
*   The topmost component is the menu bar. To create a menu bar, call JMenuBar's constructor with no parameter values. For example, to create a menu bar called *menuBar*, use:

```
JMenuBar menuBar = new JMenuBar();
```

*   Add a menu bar to the window or a panel with JFrame's *add()* method or JPanel's *add()* method.
*   The next level of component in a menu bar is a menu. A menu places clickable text on the menu bar. To create a menu, call JMenu's constructor with a string parameter value, the text to display on the menu bar. You can then add the menu to a menu bar with JMenuBar's *add()* method. For example, to create a menu called *helpMenu*, with text “Help”, and add *helpMenu* to *menuBar*, use:

```
JMenu helpMenu = new JMenu("Help");
menuBar.add(helpMenu);
```

*   Create a menu for each option you want on the menu bar.
*   Complete a menu bar using menu items. Menu items appear in a drop-down list of clickable texts from a menu. To create a menu item, call JMenuItem's constructor with a string parameter value: the text to display in the menu list. You can then add the menu item to a menu with JMenu's *add()* method. For example, to create a menu item called *aboutMenuItem*, with text “About”, and add *aboutMenuItem* to *helpMenu,* use:

```
JMenuItem aboutMenuItem = new JMenuItem("About");
menuBar.add(aboutMenuItem);
```

*   Create a menu item for each clickable text item you want on the drop down list from a menu.
*   You can add separators between menu items in a menu with JMenu's *addSeparator()* method. To add a separator in *helpMenu*, use:

```
helpMenu.addSeparator();
```

*   Add functionality to a menu or a menu item by adding an action listener the same way you add an action listener to a button: use JMenu's *addActionListener()* method or JMenuItem's *addActionListener()* method, with a new ActionListener object as the parameter value. In the ActionListener, add a public method called *actionPerformed()*. *actionPerformed()* should have one parameter, an ActionEvent, and return nothing. For example, to add an action listener to a menu item called *aboutMenuItem* to call *displayAbout()* when the button is clicked, use:

```
aboutMenuItem.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
	public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
		displayAbout();
	}
});
```

### Key Points and More

*   A file chooser is a complete dialog that lets the user choose a file on his computer. To create a file chooser, create a new JFileChooser object, passing no parameter values.
*   To open the file chooser dialog, call JFileChooser's *showOpenDialog()* method, with *this* as the parameter value. If the user selected a file, the method will return JFileChooser's *APPROVE_OPTION* variable. If he canceled the dialog, the method will return JFileChooser's *CANCEL_OPTION* variable.
*   To get the file the user chose, use JFileChooser's *getSelectedFile()* method. This will be a File object you can use wherever File objects are expected. If you need the name of the file, use File's *getName()* method.
*   For example, to create a file chooser called *chooser*, display *chooser*, and put the selected file into a new File called *file*, use:

```
JFileChooser chooser = new JFileChooser();
int option = chooser.showOpenDialog(this);
if(option == JFileChooser.APPROVE_OPTION) {
	File file = chooser.getSelectedFile();
```

*   You can set the initial folder for the file chooser when you call the JFileChooser's constructor. You may use a string that is the full path and name of the file. Or you may use a File object created using a file that is in the folder you want to open. Using a File as a parameter value to the JFileChooser's constructor will be demonstrated in a later lesson.
*   To name a default selected file when the dialog opens, use JFileChooser's *setSelectedFile()* method with the File object to select. This will be demonstrated in a later lesson.
*   JFileChooser's *showOpenDialog()* method uses “Open” as the text on the approve button. JFileChooser's *showSaveDialog()* method uses “Save” as the text on the approve button. You could instead use JFileChooser's *showDialog()* method and provide any other text you want displayed on the approve button. A save dialog will be demonstrated in a later lesson.

### Key Points and More

*   Use a file filter if you want to restrict which files will be in a file chooser's file list.
*   Create a file filter by extending the FileFilter class.
*   A file filter has to have a public method called *getDescription()*. It should take no parameters and return a string: the text that you want in the file type field of the FileChooser dialog.
*   A file filter also has to have a public method called *accept()*. It should take one parameter, a File, and return a boolean. *accept* should return *true* if you want that file included in the list of choices and *false* if you don't want it included.
*   To check whether a File has an extension you want, get the file name with File's *getName()* method. Convert the name to lower case with String's *toLowerCase()* method. Then check whether the lower case string ends with an extension you want with String's *endsWith()* method.
*   Do you want to allow the user to select a file from a different folder? If so, the *accept()* method should also allow folders in the list. To check whether the file is a folder, use File's *isDirectory()* method.
    *   If the user tries to open a folder in a FileChooser dialog, the dialog will show the contents of the selected folder and wait for the user to select a file. Even though the *accept()* method accepts folders, the FileChooser dialog will only return files, not folders.
*   For example, to create a file filter class called *TextFilter* that will accept only files that end with “.txt”, but allows the user to search other folders, use:

```
public class TextFileFilter extends FileFilter {
	public String getDescription() {
		return "Text Files: *.txt";
	}
	public boolean accept(File file) {
		boolean accept = false;
		String fileName = file.getName().toLowerCase();
		if(fileName.endsWith(".txt")
				|| file.isDirectory()) {
			accept = true;
		}
		return accept;
	}
}
```

*   Set the file filter for a file chooser with FileChooser's *setFileFilter()* method. For example, to create a TextFileFilter object called *filter* and set *filter* as the file filter for a FileChooser called *chooser*, use:

```
TextFileFilter filter = new TextFileFilter();
chooser.setFileFilter(filter);
```

### Key Points and More

*   One of Graphics' *drawImage()* methods can scale an image. This *drawImage() method* takes ten parameter values:
    *   The first three parameter values are the same as you've used for *drawImage()* before: the image you're drawing and the x and y coordinates of where you want the image drawn on *g*.
    *   The next two parameter values are the width and height you want for the new image on *g*.
    *   The next four parameter values are the x and y coordinates, and width and height, of the image you're copying from.
    *   The final parameter value is the same ImageObserver parameter value you've used before.
*   For example, if you want to draw a 1600 pixel wide and 1200 pixel high area of an image called *bigImage*, starting at position 100 from the left edge and 200 from the top, to a 640 pixel wide and 480 pixel high area of *g* at position 10, 20 of *g*, use:

```
g.drawImage(bigImage, 10, 20, 640, 480, 100, 200, 1600, 1200, this);
```

*   In the previous programs in this book, you had only used Graphics in the *paintComponent()* method. But you can also get the Graphics object of any BufferedImage object.
*   Once you get the Graphics object for a BufferedImage object, you can draw on the the Graphics object with any of the Graphics methods. All drawings on the Graphics object will be done on the image itself. When you're done drawing on the Graphics object, dispose of the Graphics object by calling Graphihc's *dispose()* method. Any drawing you did with the Graphics object will remain on the image.
*   For example, to draw the text “Happy Birthday!” at position 10, 20 of a BufferedImage called *photo*, you need to get BufferedImage's Graphics object, draw the text, and dispose of the Graphics object, like this:

```
Graphics g = photo.getGraphics();
g.drawString("Happy Birthday!", 10, 20);
g.dispose();
```

*   *   Drawing strings will be explained in more detail in a later lesson.

*   You can change your program to use the system look and feel. The program will then look more like other programs being run on that particular operating system, whether it be Windows, OS X, or Linux.

```
try {
	String className = UIManager.getSystemLookAndFeelClassName();
	UIManager.setLookAndFeel(className);
}
catch (Exception e) {}
```

*   You should decide which is more important to you: having your program look the same on every computer or having your program match the look and feel of each operating system. If your program looks the same on every operating system, you will know everyone will see the program exactly the way you do, but the program user may not be as comfortable using the program. If the program matches the look and feel of each operating system, the user may be more comfortable using the program, but the resulting layout could sometimes look bad without your knowledge.

# Project 9 - Greedy

Greedy is a dice game where the player tries to reach the highest possible score in ten rounds. He may increase his score by rolling the dice as many times as he wants in each round. But he dare not be too greedy. If he has a bad roll, he could lose all his points for that round!

The game starts by rolling all six dice. If any dice show points, and the player chooses to end the round, he keeps the points he's rolled so far. Or the player may choose to roll the remaining dice to see whether he can earn more points for that round. If he rolls additional points, he may end the round or roll any dice still remaining. If he's lucky enough for all six dice to have points, he may roll all six dice again. He must continue to choose between ending the round or rolling the remaining dice. However, if at any point he gets no additional points by rolling the remaining dice, he loses all the points he's accumulated for that round, and the round ends.

Points are scored as follows:

*   Each one (unless three or more are rolled together) - 10 points
*   Each five (unless three or more are rolled together) - 5 points
*   Three ones - 100 points
*   Three of anything else - 10 times the value of the die. For example, three sixes would be 60 points
*   Four of a kind - 200 points
*   Five of a kind - 300 points
*   Six of a kind - 500 points
*   Straight (one through six) - 250 points

Here is a screenshot of the Greedy program:

![](images/00010.jpeg)

### Key Points and More

*   Buttons can only display text or images. Use a panel instead of a button if you want to paint the clickable image yourself. However, panels don't recognize mouse clicks unless a mouse listener is added.
*   To add a mouse listener to a panel, use JPanel's *addMouseListener()* method.
*   To add a mouse listener, add a MouseAdapter object instead of a MouseListener object. MouseAdapter extends MouseListener, so may be used anywhere MouseListener is allowed. Much less code is required for a MouseAdapter object than for a MouseListener object.
*   To get a new MouseAdapter to recognize when a mouse is clicked, add one of three public methods:
    *   *mousePressed()* - will run when the mouse button is pressed. Use this method if you want to make sure the event happens where the mouse is pressed down. (Note, if the user drags the mouse, *mousePressed()* and *mouseReleased()* won't happen at the same place.) This method will be used in later lessons.
    *   *mouseReleased()* - will run when the mouse button is released. Use this method if you want to make sure the event doesn't happen until the click is complete.
    *   *mouseClicked()* - will run when the mouse button is pressed and released and not moved between actions. Though this seems like the better choice for checking if a mouse was clicked, many people find this doesn't work very well. If the mouse is accidentally dragged even a tiny bit, the event won't happen.
*   Each of the above three methods must have one parameter, a MouseEvent, and return nothing. For example, to add a mouse listener that calls *click()* when the mouse is pressed, use:

```
addMouseListener(new MouseAdapter() {
	public void mousePressed(MouseEvent e) {
		click();
	}
});
```

*   Mouse events and mouse movement will be covered in more detail in later lessons.

## Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts

A box layout arranges components into a single row or column. By combining panels with different box layout options, you can arrange components in complex ways.

A box layout may stretch some components to fill the width or height of the panel.

### Key Points and More

*   A JFrame defaults to using a BorderLayout. Use this layout to easily to put a title at the top of the window, a button panel at the bottom of the window, and the main panel in the center of the window.
*   A JPanel defaults to using a FlowLayout. Use a FlowLayout to diplay a row of components, at their preferred size and centered in the panel. The button panel works well with FlowLayout. However, keep in mind that if you add more components than will fit the width of the panel, FlowLayout will flow additional components to another row.
*   If you need rows and columns of components all the same size, use a GridLayout.
*   If you have an assortment of components of various sizes that you want arranged in the window, try to organize the components into rows or columns of panels that contain rows or columns of components. Each panel could then use a BoxLayout. A BoxLayout is how the many different components were arranged in the center panel of the Greedy program.
*   To create a BoxLayout object, call BoxLayout's constructor, with the component for which you are creating the layout, and either BoxLayout's X_AXIS or Y_AXIS variable.
    *   X_AXIS - lay out the components along the [x-axis](#part0003_split_082.html_x-axis) (in a row).
    *   Y_AXIS - lay out the components along the y-axis (in a column).
*   To add BoxLayout to a panel, call JPanel's *setLayout()* method, with a BoxLayout as the parameter value. For example, to create a new Box Layout object that will arrange the components in a column on a JPanel called *infoPanel*, use:

```
infoPanel.setLayout(new BoxLayout(infoPanel, BoxLayout.Y_AXIS));
```

*   In a BoxLayout with y-axis, components are displayed in a column at their preferred height. Components will be displayed at the panel's full width if the panel's width is less than the component's maximum width.
*   If a component's maximum width is less than the panel's width, use the component's *setAlignmentX()* method to change to left, right, or center alignment. For example, to center a JLabel called *title* in a panel with a BoxLayout, use:

```
title.setAlignmentX(JLabel.CENTER_ALIGNMENT);
```

*   In a BoxLayout with x-axis, components are displayed in a row at their preferred width. Components will be displayed at the panel's full height if the panel's height is less than the component's maximum height.
*   If a component's maximum height is less than the panel's height, use the component's *setAlignmentY()* method to change to top, bottom, or center alignment.
*   JLabel has methods called *setAlignmentX()* and *setHorizontalAlignment()*. What's the difference? *setHorizontalAlignment()* centers the text within the label. *setAlignmentX()* sets the alignment of the label within the panel. If a label is smaller than the panel, even if the text is centered in the label, the label won't appear centered if the label is not centered in the panel. Using JLabel's *setHorizontalAlignment()* method was covered in an earlier lesson.

### Key Points and More

*   A text field is an editable field where the program user can enter text.
*   Create a text field by creating a JTextField object.
*   You can get the text from a JTextField object's text field, using JTextField's *getText()* method.
*   You can change the text in a text field, with JTextField's *setText()* method.
*   Depending on the layout of the panel to which the text field is added, the text field will either be as wide as the panel or a width that depends on the field's preferred size. The default preferred size of a text field is calculated using the number of columns set in the constructor and the [font metrics](#part0003_split_082.html_font-metrics) of the font being used for the field's text.
*   This project demonstrated that the default panel layout, FlowLayout, calculated the width of the JTextField, based on the number of columns set in the constructor and the field's preferred size, and that BoxLayout made the JTextField as wide as the panel.
*   You can also set initial text in a field by using a string parameter value in the constructor, as will be demonstrated in a later lesson.
*   A radio button is a clickable button that is either selected or unselected. A radio button is displayed as a small round button to the left of the radio button's text.
*   Create a radio button by calling JRadioButton's constructor with the text for the button.
*   If only one of several radio button should be selected at a time, those radio buttons should be put into a button group. Create a button group by creating a ButtonGroup object. Selecting one radio button in a group automatically deselects a previously selected radio button in the same group. Create a separate ButtonGroup object for each group of radio buttons.
*   You can set a radio button as selected by calling JRadioButton's *setSelected()* method.
*   You can check whether a radio button is selected by calling JRadioButton's *isSelected()* method.

### Key Points and More

*   Provide public methods to get the information that the user entered in the dialog.
*   A modal dialog is a dialog that can remain open and usable as the user continues working with other windows in the program.

*   If your program should wait for input from the user before continuing, the program will need to open a non-modal dialog.
