The program can then be [run](#part0003_split_082.html_run) without Eclipse by double-clicking on the name of the [JAR file](#part0003_split_082.html_JAR-file). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 2.2 - Export a Program* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See [*Export a Program*](#part0003_split_094.html_Export-a-Program) in [*Appendix D - Using Eclipse*](#part0003_split_089.html_Appendix-D---Using-Eclipse).

**extend**

A [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) may already exist that provides functionality close to that needed for a new [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class). Instead of adding more [variables](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) and [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) to the first [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class), and instead of repeating all the first [class's](#part0003_split_082.html_class) [variables](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) and [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) in the new class, [define](#part0003_split_082.html_define) the new [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) to extend the first [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class). The original [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) then serves as the [superclass](#part0003_split_082.html_superclass) of the new [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**extract**

Extracting files is the process of copying and [decompressing](#part0003_split_082.html_compress) the files that are stored in a [ZIP file](#part0003_split_082.html_ZIP-file) or [JAR file](#part0003_split_082.html_JAR-file) into another folder on the computer. See [*Download and Install Eclipse*](#part0003_split_087.html_Download-and-Install-Eclipse) in [*Appendix C - Setup*](#part0003_split_084.html_Appendix-C---Setup). See [*Download MoreDIYJava.zip Detailed Instructions*](#part0003_split_088.html_Download-MoreDIYJava.zip-Detailed-Instructions) in [*Appendix C - Setup*](#part0003_split_084.html_Appendix-C---Setup).

**File**

The Java File [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) allows programs to work with the contents of a file and its path name. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_039.html_kp6.2) in [*Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons*](#part0003_split_038.html_Lesson-6.2---Read-Image-Files,-Subimages,-Image-Icons). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_047.html_kp8.2) in [*Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers*](#part0003_split_046.html_Lesson-8.2---File-Choosers). See [*Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts*](#part0003_split_052.html_Lesson-9.2---Box-Layout,-Combined-Layouts).

**file chooser**

A file chooser is a [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog) that allows the [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) to browse through a list of files on his computer and choose a file to use in the program. Create a file chooser using [JFileChooser](#part0003_split_082.html_JFileChooser). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_047.html_kp8.2) in [*Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers*](#part0003_split_046.html_Lesson-8.2---File-Choosers).

**file filter**

A file filter applied to a [file chooser](#part0003_split_082.html_file-chooser) will restrict the files in the chooser's list by some criteria. For example, a file filter could be added to include only those files with a specific file name extension. Create a file filter using the [FileFilter](#part0003_split_082.html_FileFilter) class. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_048.html_kp8.3) in [*Lesson 8.3 - An Image File Filter*](#part0003_split_047.html_Lesson-8.3---An-Image-File-Filter).

**FileFilter**

FileFilter is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that should be extended to create a [file filter](#part0003_split_082.html_file-filter). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_048.html_kp8.3) in [*Lesson 8.3 - An Image File Filter*](#part0003_split_047.html_Lesson-8.3---An-Image-File-Filter).

**FileNotFoundException**

A FileNotFoundException is an [exception](#part0003_split_082.html_exception) [thrown](#part0003_split_082.html_throw-an-exception) when the program tries to read from a file that does not exist. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**FileReader**

A FileReader reads [character](#part0003_split_082.html_character) data from a file. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**FileWriter**

A FileWriter writes character data to a file. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**final**

The value of a [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) with the [final](#part0003_split_082.html_final) attribute is set and then never changed by the program. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 14.6 - Static Final Variables* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**float**

Float is a basic data type in Java. A float variable can hold a decimal number with as many as 7 decimal places. To use a float value in a program, type the value with a decimal point, add an “f” to the end of the value, and use no quotes. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.6 - Double Data Type* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**FlowLayout**

The FlowLayout is a [layout](#part0003_split_082.html_layout) best used whenever any number of [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) should be arranged in a row, and each displayed at its [preferred size](#part0003_split_082.html_preferred-size). However, additional rows will be created in a FlowLayout if not all the [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) fit within the width of the [container](#part0003_split_082.html_container). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_019.html_kp2.3) in [*Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension*](#part0003_split_018.html_Lesson-2.3---Multiple-Panels,-Preferred-Size,-Dimension).

**focus**

The [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) in focus will receive [keyboard input](#part0003_split_082.html_keyboard-input). Only one [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) will be in focus at a time. Focus is often referred to as keyboard focus. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_036.html_kp5.2) in [*Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark*](#part0003_split_035.html_Lesson-5.2---In-Focus-Mark). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_044.html_kp7.3) in [*Lesson 7.3 - Button Focus*](#part0003_split_043.html_Lesson-7.3---Button-Focus). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_072.html_kp12.3) in [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners).

**focus listener**

Focus listeners are [classes](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that [extend](#part0003_split_082.html_extend) the [FocusListener](#part0003_split_082.html_FocusListener) [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class). They wait for [FocusEvents](#part0003_split_082.html_FocusEvent). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_072.html_kp12.3) in [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners).

**focus mark**

Focus mark refers to the mark that gets painted on a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) when the [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) is in [focus](#part0003_split_082.html_focus). For example, a [button](#part0003_split_082.html_button) will have a rectangle painted around the button's text when the button is in [focus](#part0003_split_082.html_focus). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_036.html_kp5.2) in [*Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark*](#part0003_split_035.html_Lesson-5.2---In-Focus-Mark).

**FocusAdapter**

A FocusAdapter is a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that makes creating a [FocusListener](#part0003_split_082.html_FocusListener) [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object) easier. Using a FocusAdapter, a programmer writes [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) only for the [FocusListener's](#part0003_split_082.html_FocusListener) [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined FocusListener methods. A FocusAdapter may be used wherever a [FocusListener](#part0003_split_082.html_FocusListener) is required. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_072.html_kp12.3) in [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners).

**FocusEvent**

A FocusEvent is an [event](#part0003_split_082.html_event) caused by a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) coming into [focus](#part0003_split_082.html_focus) or going out of [focus](#part0003_split_082.html_focus). Add a [FocusListener](#part0003_split_082.html_FocusListener) to a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) to [run](#part0003_split_082.html_run) [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) when the FocusEvent occurs. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_072.html_kp12.3) in [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners).

**FocusListener**

A FocusListener waits for a [FocusEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_FocusEvent) from its assigned [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component). When a [FocusEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_FocusEvent) occurs, Java [calls](#part0003_split_082.html_call) the FocusListener's *focusGained()* or *focusLost()* [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_072.html_kp12.3) in [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners).

**font**

A font [defines](#part0003_split_082.html_define) how characters will be drawn to the display. A font [defines](#part0003_split_082.html_define) the type design, style, and size of the characters. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_008.html_kp1.3) in [*Lesson 1.3 - Font*](#part0003_split_007.html_Lesson-1.3---Font). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_063.html_kp11.2) in [*Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics*](#part0003_split_062.html_Lesson-11.2---Draw-Strings,-Font-Metrics).

**font metrics**

Font metrics are the measurements of how text is rendered in a specific [font](#part0003_split_082.html_font). A font metrics [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object) can calculate the measurements of text, or of portions of character symbols. Use [FontMetrics](#part0003_split_082.html_FontMetrics) to create font metrics. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_063.html_kp11.2) in [*Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics*](#part0003_split_062.html_Lesson-11.2---Draw-Strings,-Font-Metrics).

**FontMetrics**

FontMetrics is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used to create a [font metrics](#part0003_split_082.html_font-metrics) [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_063.html_kp11.2) in [*Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics*](#part0003_split_062.html_Lesson-11.2---Draw-Strings,-Font-Metrics).

**for loop**

A *for* loop is a [block of code](#part0003_split_082.html_block-of-code) that repeats a set number of times. A *for* loop typically [initializes](#part0003_split_082.html_initialize) an [iteration variable](#part0003_split_082.html_iteration-variable), [increments](#part0003_split_082.html_increment) or [decrements](#part0003_split_082.html_decrement) the iteration variable, and [terminates](#part0003_split_082.html_terminate) when the [iteration variable](#part0003_split_082.html_iteration-variable) reaches a particular value. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 11.1 - For Loops* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**foreground color**

The foreground color is the [color](#part0003_split_082.html_color) used for the text or symbols that are drawn onto a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component). For example, the circle for a [radio button](#part0003_split_082.html_radio-button) will be drawn in the foreground color. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_020.html_kp2.4) in [*Lesson 2.4 - Foreground Color*](#part0003_split_019.html_Lesson-2.4---Foreground-Color).

**format**

Format refers to the way items are arranged or to a pattern. For example, [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) may be formatted with [blocks of code](#part0003_split_082.html_block-of-code) indented, or a date may be formatted using two-digit values for month, day, and year, each separated with a forward slash.

**glue component**

Glue components are often added to a [container](#part0003_split_082.html_container) with [BoxLayout](#part0003_split_082.html_BoxLayout), to add space between other [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component). Glue components are invisible and will stretch in size equally to use up any extra space in that row or column. To add an exact amount of space that won't stretch, use a [rigid component](#part0003_split_082.html_rigid-component) instead. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_064.html_kp11.3) in [*Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components*](#part0003_split_063.html_Lesson-11.3---Space-Between-Components). See [*Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window*](#part0003_split_065.html_Lesson-11.5---Component-Listeners,-Window-State-Listeners,-Resize-a-Window).

**graphical user interface**

A graphical user interface, often abbreviated as a [GUI](#part0003_split_082.html_GUI), is a visual way for program [users](#part0003_split_082.html_user) to interact with a computer. A [GUI](#part0003_split_082.html_GUI) consists of a [window](#part0003_split_082.html_window), plus [buttons](#part0003_split_082.html_button), menus, and any other visual input methods that allow a [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) to express what he wants the program to do. See [*Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout*](#part0003_split_016.html_Lesson-2.1---Border-Layout).

**graphics**

Graphics are usually any sort of visual image or design. See the [*Introduction*](#part0003_split_000.html_Introduction).

**Graphics**

The Graphics [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) allows a program to draw, [scale](#part0003_split_082.html_scale), or rotate the contents of an image, or to draw on a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_042.html_kp7.1) in [*Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size*](#part0003_split_041.html_Lesson-7.1---A-Painted-Panel:-Color,-Rectangles,-Lines,-Circles,-and-Preferred-Size). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_049.html_kp8.4) in [*Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image*](#part0003_split_048.html_Lesson-8.4---New-Graphics,-Scale-an-Image). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_063.html_kp11.2) in [*Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics*](#part0003_split_062.html_Lesson-11.2---Draw-Strings,-Font-Metrics). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_073.html_kp12.4) in [*Lesson 12.4 - XOR Mode*](#part0003_split_072.html_Lesson-12.4---XOR-Mode).

**GridLayout**

The GridLayout is a [layout](#part0003_split_082.html_layout) best used whenever [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) should be arranged in a grid, with each section the same size. If [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) are not all the same size, they will be stretched so they are displayed the same size. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_031.html_kp4.2) in [*Lesson 4.2 - Grid Layout*](#part0003_split_030.html_Lesson-4.2---Grid-Layout).

**GUI**

GUI stands for [Graphical User Interface](#part0003_split_082.html_graphical-user-interface). See [*Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout*](#part0003_split_016.html_Lesson-2.1---Border-Layout).

**hardware**

Hardware is the physical part of a computer: the hard drive, keyboard, mouse, etc. The [operating system](#part0003_split_082.html_operating-system) allows [software](#part0003_split_082.html_software) to interact with the computer hardware.

**horizontal alignment**

Use a [label's](#part0003_split_082.html_label) *setHorizontalAlignment0* [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) to horizontally align text in a [label](#part0003_split_082.html_label). Use a [container's](#part0003_split_082.html_container) *setAlignmentX()* [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) to horizontally align a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) in its [container](#part0003_split_082.html_container). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_009.html_kp1.4) in [*Lesson 1.4 - Align Text*](#part0003_split_008.html_Lesson-1.4---Align-Text). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_053.html_kp9.2) in [*Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts*](#part0003_split_052.html_Lesson-9.2---Box-Layout,-Combined-Layouts)

**if statement**

An if statement is a [block of code](#part0003_split_082.html_block-of-code) that [runs](#part0003_split_082.html_run) only if the specified test evaluates to true. An if statement may also have an optional [else block](#part0003_split_082.html_else-block) that runs only if the test evaluates to false. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**Image**

The Image [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) represents many different kinds of images. Image provides [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) that are common to all images. However, a program must first identify the Image [type](#part0003_split_082.html_type). A [BufferedImage](#part0003_split_082.html_BufferedImage) is one kind of Image. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_039.html_kp6.2) in [*Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons*](#part0003_split_038.html_Lesson-6.2---Read-Image-Files,-Subimages,-Image-Icons). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_049.html_kp8.4) in [*Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image*](#part0003_split_048.html_Lesson-8.4---New-Graphics,-Scale-an-Image). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_071.html_kp12.2) in [*Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image*](#part0003_split_070.html_Lesson-12.2---Save-an-Image).

**image button**

An image button is a [button](#part0003_split_082.html_button) that displays an image instead of text. Create an image button using [JButton](#part0003_split_082.html_JButton) with an [ImageIcon](#part0003_split_082.html_ImageIcon). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_038.html_kp6.1) in [*Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images*](#part0003_split_037.html_Lesson-6.1---Buttons-with-Images). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_070.html_kp12.1) in [*Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars*](#part0003_split_069.html_Lesson-12.1---Toolbars)

**image label**

An image label is a [label](#part0003_split_082.html_label) that displays an image instead of text. Create an image label using [JLabel](#part0003_split_082.html_JLabel) with an [ImageIcon](#part0003_split_082.html_ImageIcon). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_070.html_kp12.1) in [*Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars*](#part0003_split_069.html_Lesson-12.1---Toolbars).

**ImageIcon**

ImageIcon is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) for images used in [buttons](#part0003_split_082.html_button) and [labels](#part0003_split_082.html_label). An ImageIcon object is typically a small image and is easily loaded into the program using the file name or URL. An ImageIcon is not a type of [Image](#part0003_split_082.html_Image), so an ImageIcon may not be used where [Images](#part0003_split_082.html_Image) are expected, nor may an [Image](#part0003_split_082.html_Image) be used where an ImageIcon is expected. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_038.html_kp6.1) in [*Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images*](#part0003_split_037.html_Lesson-6.1---Buttons-with-Images). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_039.html_kp6.2) in [*Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons*](#part0003_split_038.html_Lesson-6.2---Read-Image-Files,-Subimages,-Image-Icons). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_070.html_kp12.1) in [*Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars*](#part0003_split_069.html_Lesson-12.1---Toolbars). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_071.html_kp12.2) in [*Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image*](#part0003_split_070.html_Lesson-12.2---Save-an-Image).

**ImageIO**

ImageIO is a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) for reading and writing image files of various types. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_039.html_kp6.2) in [*Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons*](#part0003_split_038.html_Lesson-6.2---Read-Image-Files,-Subimages,-Image-Icons). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_071.html_kp12.2) in [*Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image*](#part0003_split_070.html_Lesson-12.2---Save-an-Image). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_076.html_kp13.1) in [*Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images*](#part0003_split_075.html_Lesson-13.1---Transparent-Colors,-PNG-Images).

**import**

Java must have the full, proper name of every [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) it uses in a program, including the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) [package](#part0003_split_082.html_package) name. Import [statements](#part0003_split_082.html_statement) give the full name of all non-standard [classes](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used in the program, so that those [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) names may be used later without their [package](#part0003_split_082.html_package) names. Import a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) by adding an import [statement](#part0003_split_082.html_statement) for that [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) at the beginning of the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) [definition](#part0003_split_082.html_define). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**increment**

To increment a variable, increase its value by a small amount, usually 1\. *See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.3 - Increment Integers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**index**

An index is the position of an item in an ordered collection of items. For example, indexes are used to name the position of a [character](#part0003_split_082.html_character) in a [string](#part0003_split_082.html_string), or an element in an array. The [iteration variable](#part0003_split_082.html_iteration-variable) in a [*for* loop](#part0003_split_082.html_for-loop) is sometimes referred to as the loop index. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 13.4 - Index of Characters in a String* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 15.3 - Index of Next Character* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**initialize**

To initialize a [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable), assign its first value. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**input**

Input used as a noun is data that the [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) enters into a program while the program is [running](#part0003_split_082.html_run). Input is used as a verb when a [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) inputs his data into a program. Input is also the name of a [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method): input(). The text-based programs from *Do-It-Yourself Java Games* [call](#part0003_split_082.html_call) *input()* to wait for the [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) to enter his data. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 4.1 - Input a String* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 15.4 - Check User Input* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**input field**

An input field is a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) that allows a program [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) to enter character data to be used by a program. Create an input field using [JTextField](#part0003_split_082.html_JTextField) or [JTextArea](#part0003_split_082.html_JTextArea). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_027.html_kp3.1) in [*Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas*](#part0003_split_026.html_Lesson-3.1---Text-Areas). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_056.html_kp10.2) in [*Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons*](#part0003_split_055.html_Lesson-10.2---Text-Fields,-Radio-Buttons). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_070.html_kp12.1) in [*Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars*](#part0003_split_069.html_Lesson-12.1---Toolbars). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_072.html_kp12.3) in [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners).

**input stream**

An input stream reads non-character data from a file. Create an input stream using [InputStream](#part0003_split_082.html_InputStream). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_068.html_kp11.7) in [*Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File*](#part0003_split_067.html_Lesson-11.7---Put-Data-Files-in-the-JAR-File).

**InputStream**

The InputStream [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) is used to create an [input stream](#part0003_split_082.html_input-stream) of non-character data. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_068.html_kp11.7) in [*Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File*](#part0003_split_067.html_Lesson-11.7---Put-Data-Files-in-the-JAR-File).

**InputStreamReader**

The InputStreamReader [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) is used to read non-character data from an [input stream](#part0003_split_082.html_input-stream) and convert it into character data. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_068.html_kp11.7) in [*Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File*](#part0003_split_067.html_Lesson-11.7---Put-Data-Files-in-the-JAR-File).

**instance**

A [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) is a [definition](#part0003_split_082.html_define) of an [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object). An [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object), or [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) instance, is created from a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) [definition](#part0003_split_082.html_define). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 16.1 - Objects, Card* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**instance variable**

An instance variable is a [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) in a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) [definition](#part0003_split_082.html_define) instead of in a [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method). Such a [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) may be used by any of the [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) defined by that [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class), without the variable being [passed](#part0003_split_082.html_pass) to the [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) as a [parameter value](#part0003_split_082.html_parameter-value). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**int**

Int is a basic data type in Java. An int [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) can hold an [integer](#part0003_split_082.html_integer) value between -2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,647\. To use an int value in a program, type the value without quotes. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**integer**

An integer is a whole number value, either positive or negative. An integer value is typed without quotes or a decimal point. Integer [variables](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) are [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) in Java as “[int](#part0003_split_082.html_int)”, “[byte](#part0003_split_082.html_byte)”, “[short](#part0003_split_082.html_short)”, or “[long](#part0003_split_082.html_long)”. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.2 - Convert a String to an Integer* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.5 - Integer Subtraction, Multiplication, and Division* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**invalid**

If something, for example data provided by a user, is invalid, it is not [valid](#part0003_split_082.html_valid), not allowed. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 15.4 - Check User Input* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**IOException**

An IOException is an [exception](#part0003_split_082.html_exception) [thrown](#part0003_split_082.html_throw-an-exception) when an error occurs as a program tries to read from or write to a file. For example, the IOException is [thrown](#part0003_split_082.html_throw-an-exception) if a file that exists can't be opened. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**italic**

Italic text is text whose characters are displayed as sloping to the right. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_008.html_kp1.3) in [*Lesson 1.3 - Font*](#part0003_split_007.html_Lesson-1.3---Font).

**iteration variable**

An iteration variable is a [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) in a [*for* loop](#part0003_split_082.html_for-loop), [incremented](#part0003_split_082.html_increment) or [decremented](#part0003_split_082.html_decrement) each time through the loop, and compared against another value as a loop exit test. The iteration variable, sometimes also called the loop [index](#part0003_split_082.html_index) or loop control variable, is used to control the number of times the [*for* loop](#part0003_split_082.html_for-loop) runs. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 11.1 - For Loops* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**JAR file**

A JAR file is a Java Archive file. It contains one or more folders or files of Java program [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code). A JAR file is named with “.jar” as its extension. If the JAR file is created as a Java executable file, the program in the JAR file can be [run](#part0003_split_082.html_run) by simply double-clicking on the name of the JAR file. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 2.2 - Export a Program* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_068.html_kp11.7) in [*Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File*](#part0003_split_067.html_Lesson-11.7---Put-Data-Files-in-the-JAR-File).

**Java project**

The Java Project is the highest level of organization of Java [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) in Eclipse. Each program in this book is organized in a separate Java project in Eclipse. The Java project contains one or more [packages](#part0003_split_082.html_package), and each [package](#part0003_split_082.html_package) contains one or more [classes](#part0003_split_082.html_class). Because the programs are small, most of the Java projects in this book contain only one [package](#part0003_split_082.html_package). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See [*Create a First Project*](#part0003_split_090.html_Create-a-First-Project) in [*Appendix D - Using Eclipse*](#part0003_split_089.html_Appendix-D---Using-Eclipse).

**JButton**

JButton is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating [buttons](#part0003_split_082.html_button). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_023.html_kp2.7) in [*Lesson 2.7 - Buttons*](#part0003_split_022.html_Lesson-2.7---Buttons). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_030.html_kp4.1) in [*Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this*](#part0003_split_029.html_Lesson-4.1---A-Custom-Button,-this). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_035.html_kp5.1) in [*Lesson 5.1 - Another Custom Button*](#part0003_split_034.html_Lesson-5.1---Another-Custom-Button). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_038.html_kp6.1) in [*Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images*](#part0003_split_037.html_Lesson-6.1---Buttons-with-Images).

**JDialog**

JDialog is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating custom [dialogs](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_055.html_kp10.1) in [*Lesson 10.1 - A Custom Dialog*](#part0003_split_054.html_Lesson-10.1---A-Custom-Dialog).

**JFrame**

JFrame is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating [windows](#part0003_split_082.html_window). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_006.html_kp1.1) in [*Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window*](#part0003_split_005.html_Lesson-1.1---A-Standard-Window). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_007.html_kp1.2) in [*Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size*](#part0003_split_006.html_Lesson-1.2---Add-Text,-Window-Size). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_010.html_kp1.5) in [*Lesson 1.5 - Pack a Window*](#part0003_split_009.html_Lesson-1.5---Pack-a-Window). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_011.html_kp1.6) in [*Lesson 1.6 - Disable Resizing*](#part0003_split_010.html_Lesson-1.6---Disable-Resizing). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_012.html_kp1.7) in [*Lesson 1.7 - Window Title, Center*](#part0003_split_011.html_Lesson-1.7---Window-Title,-Center).

**JFileChooser**

JFileChooser is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating [file choosers](#part0003_split_082.html_file-chooser). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_047.html_kp8.2) in [*Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers*](#part0003_split_046.html_Lesson-8.2---File-Choosers).

**JLabel**

JLabel is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating [labels](#part0003_split_082.html_label). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_007.html_kp1.2) in [*Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size*](#part0003_split_006.html_Lesson-1.2---Add-Text,-Window-Size). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_070.html_kp12.1) in [*Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars*](#part0003_split_069.html_Lesson-12.1---Toolbars).

**JMenu**

JMenu is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating [menus](#part0003_split_082.html_menu). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_046.html_kp8.1) in [*Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars*](#part0003_split_045.html_Lesson-8.1---Menu-Bars).

**JMenuBar**

JMenuBar is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating a [menu bar](#part0003_split_082.html_menu-bar). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_046.html_kp8.1) in [*Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars*](#part0003_split_045.html_Lesson-8.1---Menu-Bars).

**JMenuItem**

JMenuItem is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating [menu items](#part0003_split_082.html_menu-item). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_046.html_kp8.1) in [*Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars*](#part0003_split_045.html_Lesson-8.1---Menu-Bars).

**JOptionPane**

JOptionPane is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that eases displaying [message dialogs](#part0003_split_082.html_message-dialog) or [confirm dialogs](#part0003_split_082.html_confirm-dialog). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_024.html_kp2.8) in [*Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs*](#part0003_split_023.html_Lesson-2.8---Message-Dialogs). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_033.html_kp4.4) in [*Lesson 4.4 - Confirm Dialogs*](#part0003_split_032.html_Lesson-4.4---Confirm-Dialogs).

**JPanel**

JPanel is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating [panels](#part0003_split_082.html_panel). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_018.html_kp2.2) in [*Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors*](#part0003_split_017.html_Lesson-2.2---Panels,-Predefined-Colors).

**JPEG**

JPEG is a format for image files. JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group. A JPEG file is usually named with “.jpg” as its extension. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_071.html_kp12.2) in [*Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image*](#part0003_split_070.html_Lesson-12.2---Save-an-Image). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_076.html_kp13.1) in [*Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images*](#part0003_split_075.html_Lesson-13.1---Transparent-Colors,-PNG-Images).

**JRadioButton**

JRadioButton is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating [radio buttons](#part0003_split_082.html_radio-button). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_056.html_kp10.2) in [*Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons*](#part0003_split_055.html_Lesson-10.2---Text-Fields,-Radio-Buttons).

**JScrollPane**

JScrollPane is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for adding [scroll bars](#part0003_split_082.html_scroll-bars) to any [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_028.html_kp3.2) in [*Lesson 3.2 - Scroll Bars*](#part0003_split_027.html_Lesson-3.2---Scroll-Bars).

**JTextArea**

JTextArea is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating large text fields that have multiple rows and columns. JTextAreas are usually used as [input fields](#part0003_split_082.html_input-field). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_027.html_kp3.1) in [*Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas*](#part0003_split_026.html_Lesson-3.1---Text-Areas).

**JTextField**

JTextField is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating text [input fields](#part0003_split_082.html_input-field). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_056.html_kp10.2) in [*Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons*](#part0003_split_055.html_Lesson-10.2---Text-Fields,-Radio-Buttons).

**JToolBar**

JToolBar is the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) used for creating [toolbars](#part0003_split_082.html_toolbar). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_070.html_kp12.1) in [*Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars*](#part0003_split_069.html_Lesson-12.1---Toolbars).

**key code**

The key code of a [KeyEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyEvent) is a number that represents the key on the keyboard that was pressed. Key codes are [static](#part0003_split_082.html_static) [integer](#part0003_split_082.html_integer) [variables](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) whose name starts with VK_. The key code represents which key was pressed, not the character value of the key. VK stands for virtual key. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners).

**key listener**

Key listeners are [classes](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that [extend](#part0003_split_082.html_extend) the [KeyListener](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyListener) [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class). They wait for [KeyEvents](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyEvent). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners).

**KeyAdapter**

A KeyAdapter is a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that makes creating a [KeyListener](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyListener) [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object) easier. Using a KeyAdapter, a programmer writes [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) only for the [KeyListener's](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyListener) [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined KeyListener methods. A KeyAdapter may be used wherever a [KeyListener](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyListener) is required. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners).

**keyboard input**

Keyboard input refers to data that comes to a program as a results of a [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) pressing keys on a keyboard. [Input fields](#part0003_split_082.html_input-field) could be used for keyboard input. Or a [key listener](#part0003_split_082.html_key-listener) could be created to [listen](#part0003_split_082.html_listen) for keyboard input. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_056.html_kp10.2) in [*Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons*](#part0003_split_055.html_Lesson-10.2---Text-Fields,-Radio-Buttons).

**KeyEvent**

A KeyEvent is an [event](#part0003_split_082.html_event) caused by a program user pressing a key on a keyboard. Add a [KeyListener](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyListener) to a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) to [run](#part0003_split_082.html_run) [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) when the KeyEvent occurs. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners).

**KeyListener**

A KeyListener waits for a [KeyEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyEvent) from its assigned [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component). When a [KeyEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_KeyEvent) occurs, Java [calls](#part0003_split_082.html_call) the KeyListener's *keyPressed()*, *keyReleased(),* or *keyTyped()* [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners).

**keystroke**

A keystroke is the act of pressing a keyboard key. Programs can process data about a keystroke that includes any modifiers added to the key, such as Alt, Ctrl, Shift, or mouse [button](#part0003_split_082.html_button) down. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners).

**label**

A label usually consists of a single line of text displayed in a [container](#part0003_split_082.html_container). However, an image or a combination of both image and text can also serve as a label. Create a label using [JLabel](#part0003_split_082.html_JLabel). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_007.html_kp1.2) in [*Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size*](#part0003_split_006.html_Lesson-1.2---Add-Text,-Window-Size). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_070.html_kp12.1) in [*Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars*](#part0003_split_069.html_Lesson-12.1---Toolbars).

**layout**

A [container's](#part0003_split_082.html_container) layout [defines](#part0003_split_082.html_define) how [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) will be arranged in the [container](#part0003_split_082.html_container). Java calculates the best fit, considering each [component's](#part0003_split_082.html_component) size, the layout chosen, and the system's [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define) [look and feel](#part0003_split_082.html_look-and-feel). Layouts covered in this book include [BorderLayout](#part0003_split_082.html_BorderLayout), [BoxLayout](#part0003_split_082.html_BoxLayout), [FlowLayout](#part0003_split_082.html_FlowLayout), and [GridLayout](#part0003_split_082.html_GridLayout). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_017.html_kp2.1) in [*Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout*](#part0003_split_016.html_Lesson-2.1---Border-Layout). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_019.html_kp2.3) in [*Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension*](#part0003_split_018.html_Lesson-2.3---Multiple-Panels,-Preferred-Size,-Dimension). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_031.html_kp4.2) in [*Lesson 4.2 - Grid Layout*](#part0003_split_030.html_Lesson-4.2---Grid-Layout). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_053.html_kp9.2) in [*Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts*](#part0003_split_052.html_Lesson-9.2---Box-Layout,-Combined-Layouts).

**liability**

Liability refers to responsibility for what happens. A liability disclaimer is a statement denying responsibility for any potential outcome. See [*Project 3 - Wizard of Yes/No Disclaimer*](#part0003_split_025.html_Project-3---Wizard-of-Yes/No-Disclaimer).

**library**

Eclipse refers to external [JAR files](#part0003_split_082.html_JAR-file) as libraries. For example, DIYJava.jar is a [JAR file](#part0003_split_082.html_JAR-file) that must be added as a library in the [build path](#part0003_split_082.html_build-path) of any [Java project](#part0003_split_082.html_Java-project) that uses the DIYWindow [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class). See *Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**listen**

Program [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) listens for a user action on a component, waiting for a specific kind of [event](#part0003_split_082.html_event). Each type of action requires a different [listener](#part0003_split_082.html_listener). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_023.html_kp2.7) in [*Lesson 2.7 - Buttons*](#part0003_split_022.html_Lesson-2.7---Buttons). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_032.html_kp4.3) in [*Lesson 4.3 - Event Source*](#part0003_split_031.html_Lesson-4.3---Event-Source). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_052.html_kp9.1) in [*Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners*](#part0003_split_051.html_Lesson-9.1---Mouse-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_066.html_kp11.5) in [*Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window*](#part0003_split_065.html_Lesson-11.5---Component-Listeners,-Window-State-Listeners,-Resize-a-Window). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_072.html_kp12.3) in [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_074.html_kp12.5) in [*Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners*](#part0003_split_073.html_Lesson-12.5---Draw-with-a-Mouse,-Mouse-Motion-Listeners).

**listener**

A listener is [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) written to [listen](#part0003_split_082.html_listen) for [events](#part0003_split_082.html_event). Different kinds of [events](#part0003_split_082.html_event), such as when a program [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) clicks a mouse [button](#part0003_split_082.html_button), may be recognized by different listeners, such as a [mouse listener](#part0003_split_082.html_mouse-listener). Each [type](#part0003_split_082.html_type) of listener is [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define) in a separate [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class), such as a [MouseListener](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseListener). Each [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) provides different [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) for processing an [event](#part0003_split_082.html_event), such as *mousePressed()* or *mouseReleased()*. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_023.html_kp2.7) in [*Lesson 2.7 - Buttons*](#part0003_split_022.html_Lesson-2.7---Buttons). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_052.html_kp9.1) in [*Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners*](#part0003_split_051.html_Lesson-9.1---Mouse-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_066.html_kp11.5) in [*Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window*](#part0003_split_065.html_Lesson-11.5---Component-Listeners,-Window-State-Listeners,-Resize-a-Window). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_072.html_kp12.3) in [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_074.html_kp12.5) in [*Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners*](#part0003_split_073.html_Lesson-12.5---Draw-with-a-Mouse,-Mouse-Motion-Listeners).

**listing**

A program listing usually shows all the program [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) in a file. The listings in this book are only partial listings, with an [ellipsis](#part0003_split_082.html_ellipsis), …, indicating where [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) from the file is not shown. See *Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See [*Appendix B - Completed Listings*](#part0003_split_082.html_Appendix-B---Completed-Listings).

**logical and operator**

The logical and operator, &&, is used to determine whether two tests both evaluate to true. If the test on the left side is false, Java does not perform the test on the right side. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**logical or operator**

The logical or operator, ||, is used to determine whether at least one of two tests evaluates to true. If the test on the left side is true, Java does not perform the test on the right side. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**long**

A long is a basic data type in Java. A long [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) can hold an [integer](#part0003_split_082.html_integer) value between -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 and 9,223,372,036,854,775,807\. To use a long value in a program, type the value without quotes. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**look and feel**

The look and feel of a system refers to how the [operating system](#part0003_split_082.html_operating-system) displays [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) and how the [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) work on the [operating system](#part0003_split_082.html_operating-system). Windows, OS X, and Linux [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) all look and behave differently. A Java programmer can set the look and feel for a program, independent of the [operating system](#part0003_split_082.html_operating-system) used to [run](#part0003_split_082.html_run) that program. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_015.html_kp1.10) in [*Lesson 1.10 - Cross Platform Look and Feel*](#part0003_split_014.html_Lesson-1.10---Cross-Platform-Look-and-Feel).

**main() method**

The *main()* method is the first [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) [called](#part0003_split_082.html_call) when a program starts. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**maximized**

When a [window](#part0003_split_082.html_window) is maximized, it fills the entire display area of the computer's monitor or screen. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_066.html_kp11.5) in [*Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window*](#part0003_split_065.html_Lesson-11.5---Component-Listeners,-Window-State-Listeners,-Resize-a-Window). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_067.html_kp11.6) in [*Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position*](#part0003_split_066.html_Lesson-11.6---Window-Size-and-Position).

**menu**

A menu is a drop down list of one or more choices, called [menu items](#part0003_split_082.html_menu-item), on a [menu bar](#part0003_split_082.html_menu-bar). Use a [JMenu](#part0003_split_082.html_JMenu) to create a menu. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_046.html_kp8.1) in [*Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars*](#part0003_split_045.html_Lesson-8.1---Menu-Bars).

**menu bar**

A menu bar is a row of one or more [menus](#part0003_split_082.html_menu), usually stretched across the top of a [container](#part0003_split_082.html_container). Use a [JMenuBar](#part0003_split_082.html_JMenuBar) to create a menu bar. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_046.html_kp8.1) in [*Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars*](#part0003_split_045.html_Lesson-8.1---Menu-Bars).

**menu item**

A menu item is a clickable choice in a [menu](#part0003_split_082.html_menu). When the menu item is clicked, an [ActionEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_ActionEvent) is sent. If the program is listening for the [event](#part0003_split_082.html_event), the program will usually respond in some way. Use a [JMenuItem](#part0003_split_082.html_JMenuItem) to create a menu item. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_046.html_kp8.1) in [*Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars*](#part0003_split_045.html_Lesson-8.1---Menu-Bars).

**message dialog**

A message dialog is a [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog) whose purpose is simply to display a message. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_024.html_kp2.8) in [*Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs*](#part0003_split_023.html_Lesson-2.8---Message-Dialogs).

**method**

A method is a named [block of code](#part0003_split_082.html_block-of-code) that can be [called](#part0003_split_082.html_call) from within the program. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 6.3 - Methods* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**millisecond**

A millisecond is 1/1000 of a second.

**minimized**

When a [window](#part0003_split_082.html_window) is minimized, it is removed from the screen but the program that displayed it is still running and accessible. In Microsoft Windows, a minimized window is displayed as an icon in the [task bar](#part0003_split_082.html_task-bar). Clicking on the window's icon in the [task bar](#part0003_split_082.html_task-bar) will return the [window](#part0003_split_082.html_window) to the display, at the window's previous size. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_066.html_kp11.5) in [*Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window*](#part0003_split_065.html_Lesson-11.5---Component-Listeners,-Window-State-Listeners,-Resize-a-Window). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_067.html_kp11.6) in [*Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position*](#part0003_split_066.html_Lesson-11.6---Window-Size-and-Position).

**modal**

A [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog) may be modal or [non-modal](#part0003_split_082.html_non-modal). When a modal [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog) is displayed, the program stops to wait for the [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) to close the [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog). Use a modal [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog) if the program should wait for [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) [input](#part0003_split_082.html_input) before proceeding. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_057.html_kp10.3) in [*Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data*](#part0003_split_056.html_Lesson-10.3---Get-Dialog-Data).

**monospaced font**

In a monospaced font, all the characters have the same width. In contrast, each character in a proportional font may have a different width. For example, in a monospaced font, such as Courier New, the letters “i” and “W” have the same width. In a proportional font, such as Times New Roman”, the letter “W” is much wider than the letter “i”. See *Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**mouse listener**

Mouse listeners are [classes](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that [extend](#part0003_split_082.html_extend) the [MouseListener](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseListener) [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class). They wait for [MouseEvents](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseEvent). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_052.html_kp9.1) in [*Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners*](#part0003_split_051.html_Lesson-9.1---Mouse-Listeners).

**mouse motion listener**

Mouse motion listeners are [classes](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that [extend](#part0003_split_082.html_extend) the [MouseMotionListener](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseMotionListener) [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class). They wait for [MouseEvents](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseEvent). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_074.html_kp12.5) in [*Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners*](#part0003_split_073.html_Lesson-12.5---Draw-with-a-Mouse,-Mouse-Motion-Listeners).

**MouseAdapter**

A MouseAdapter is a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that makes creating a [MouseListener](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseListener) [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object) easier. Using a MouseAdapter, a programmer writes [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) only for the [MouseListener's](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseListener) [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined MouseListener methods. A MouseAdapter may be used wherever a [MouseListener](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseListener) is required. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_052.html_kp9.1) in [*Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners*](#part0003_split_051.html_Lesson-9.1---Mouse-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_074.html_kp12.5) in [*Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners*](#part0003_split_073.html_Lesson-12.5---Draw-with-a-Mouse,-Mouse-Motion-Listeners).

**MouseEvent**

A MouseEvent is an [event](#part0003_split_082.html_event) caused by a program user clicking a mouse [button](#part0003_split_082.html_button). Add a [MouseListener](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseListener) or a [MouseMotionListener](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseMotionListener) to a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) to [run](#part0003_split_082.html_run) [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) when a MouseEvent occurs. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_052.html_kp9.1) in [*Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners*](#part0003_split_051.html_Lesson-9.1---Mouse-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_074.html_kp12.5) in [*Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners*](#part0003_split_073.html_Lesson-12.5---Draw-with-a-Mouse,-Mouse-Motion-Listeners).

**MouseListener**

A MouseListener waits for a [MouseEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseEvent) from its assigned [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component). When a [MouseEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseEvent) occurs, Java [calls](#part0003_split_082.html_call) the MouseListener's *mouseClicked()*, *mouseEntered()*, *mouseExited()*, *mousePressed()*, or *mouseReleased()* [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_052.html_kp9.1) in [*Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners*](#part0003_split_051.html_Lesson-9.1---Mouse-Listeners). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_074.html_kp12.5) in [*Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners*](#part0003_split_073.html_Lesson-12.5---Draw-with-a-Mouse,-Mouse-Motion-Listeners).

**MouseMotionAdapter**

A MouseMotionAdapter is a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that makes creating a [MouseMotionListener](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseMotionListener) [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object) easier. Using a MouseMotionAdapter, a programmer writes [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code) only for the [MouseMotionListener's](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseMotionListener) [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the defined MouseMotionListener methods. A MouseMotionAdapter may be used wherever a [MouseMotionListener](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseMotionListener) is required. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_074.html_kp12.5) in [*Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners*](#part0003_split_073.html_Lesson-12.5---Draw-with-a-Mouse,-Mouse-Motion-Listeners).

**MouseMotionListener**

A MouseMotionListener waits for a [MouseEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseEvent) from its assigned [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component). When a [MouseEvent](#part0003_split_082.html_MouseEvent) occurs, Java [calls](#part0003_split_082.html_call) the MouseMotionListener's *mouseDragged()* or *mouseMoved()* [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_074.html_kp12.5) in [*Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners*](#part0003_split_073.html_Lesson-12.5---Draw-with-a-Mouse,-Mouse-Motion-Listeners).

**non-modal**

A [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog) may be [modal](#part0003_split_082.html_modal) or non-modal. When a non-modal [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog) is displayed, the program continues to [run](#part0003_split_082.html_run). Use a non-modal [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog) if the program [user](#part0003_split_082.html_user) should continue interacting with the rest of the program while the [dialog](#part0003_split_082.html_dialog) is displayed. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_057.html_kp10.3) in [*Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data*](#part0003_split_056.html_Lesson-10.3---Get-Dialog-Data).

**not operator**

The not operator, !, inverts the value of a boolean or returns the complement of a test evaluation. For example, !*true* returns *false*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**null**

*null* means on [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object) has no value, not even a blank or a 0\. A program will receive an error if it tries to use a [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) whose value is *null* for anything other than to check its value. To use a *null* value in a program, type “null”, but without the quotes.

**NumberFormatException**

A NumberFormatException is an [exception](#part0003_split_082.html_exception) [thrown](#part0003_split_082.html_throw-an-exception) if a program cannot successfully [convert](#part0003_split_082.html_convert) a value to a number. For example, if a program tries to [convert](#part0003_split_082.html_convert) “abc” to a number, that program will [throw](#part0003_split_082.html_throw-an-exception) a NumberFormatException. See *Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**object**

An object is an [instance](#part0003_split_082.html_instance) of a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class). The object holds the information [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define) in the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) and can be operated on by the class's [methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 16.1 - Objects, Card* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

A Java class named Object is the base class of all Java classes. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_032.html_kp4.3) in [*Lesson 4.3 - Event Source*](#part0003_split_031.html_Lesson-4.3---Event-Source).

**opaque**

Opaque entities are solid. A user cannot see through an opaque object. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_021.html_kp2.5) in [*Lesson 2.5 - Opacity*](#part0003_split_020.html_Lesson-2.5---Opacity).

**operating system**

The operating system is the [software](#part0003_split_082.html_software) on the computer that manages how other programs interact with each other and with the [hardware](#part0003_split_082.html_hardware) of the computer. Examples of operating systems include Windows, OS X, or Linux. See [*Appendix C - Setup*](#part0003_split_084.html_Appendix-C---Setup).

**override**

Consider overriding a [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) whenever the [class's](#part0003_split_082.html_class) [superclass](#part0003_split_082.html_superclass) has a [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) that you would like to behave differently. To override a [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method), create a second [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method), with the exact same name, static modifier, [return](#part0003_split_082.html_return) [type](#part0003_split_082.html_type), and [parameters](#part0003_split_082.html_parameter) as the first [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method). The second method's visibility doesn't have to be identical, but the second method cannot be more [visible](#part0003_split_082.html_visible) than the [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) being overridden. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_043.html_kp7.2) in [*Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners*](#part0003_split_042.html_Lesson-7.2---Key-Listeners).

**pack**

Packing a [window](#part0003_split_082.html_window) tells Java to resize the window and arrange all of its [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) in the smallest possible area, considering all the components' [layouts](#part0003_split_082.html_layout) and [preferred sizes](#part0003_split_082.html_preferred-size). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_010.html_kp1.5) in [*Lesson 1.5 - Pack a Window*](#part0003_split_009.html_Lesson-1.5---Pack-a-Window).

**package**

Packages contain one or more [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) files that are typically used together. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See [*Create a First Package*](#part0003_split_091.html_Create-a-First-Package) in [*Appendix D - Using Eclipse*](#part0003_split_089.html_Appendix-D---Using-Eclipse).

**panel**

A panel is a [container](#part0003_split_082.html_container) that can hold many [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component), including other panels. Use [JPanel](#part0003_split_082.html_JPanel) to create panels. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_018.html_kp2.2) in [*Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors*](#part0003_split_017.html_Lesson-2.2---Panels,-Predefined-Colors). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_019.html_kp2.3) in [*Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension*](#part0003_split_018.html_Lesson-2.3---Multiple-Panels,-Preferred-Size,-Dimension).

Panels are also often used as drawing surfaces for program-created [objects](#part0003_split_082.html_object) for which Java has no [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component), such as dice, letter tiles, and cards. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_042.html_kp7.1) in [*Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, lines, Circles, and Preferred Size*](#part0003_split_041.html_Lesson-7.1---A-Painted-Panel:-Color,-Rectangles,-Lines,-Circles,-and-Preferred-Size).

**parameter**

[Methods](#part0003_split_082.html_method) are [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define) to expect zero or more [input](#part0003_split_082.html_input) values. These expected [input](#part0003_split_082.html_input) values are [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) in the [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) as parameters, each with a [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) [type](#part0003_split_082.html_type) and name. The [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) then uses those [variables](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) to access the [parameter values](#part0003_split_082.html_parameter-value) passed to the [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) when the [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) is [called](#part0003_split_082.html_call). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**parameter value**

A parameter value is [passed](#part0003_split_082.html_pass) into a [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) that has [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define) [parameters,](#part0003_split_082.html_parameter) when the [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) is [called](#part0003_split_082.html_call). The [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) may then use that value in its [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**pass**

Passing a value to a [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) with [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define) [parameters](#part0003_split_082.html_parameter) means the program sends the value to the [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) as a [parameter value](#part0003_split_082.html_parameter-value), when the method is called. See *Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**pixel**

The term pixel originated from the phrase “picture element”. A pixel is the smallest possible element of a picture. In Java, pixel refers to the smallest point [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define) for an image or the screen. For example, an image whose resolution is 640 by 480 is made up of 640 rows and 480 columns of pixels.

**PNG**

PNG is a format for image files. “PNG” stands for Portable Network [Graphics](#part0003_split_082.html_graphics). A PNG file is usually named with “.png” as its extension. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_076.html_kp13.1) in [*Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images*](#part0003_split_075.html_Lesson-13.1---Transparent-Colors,-PNG-Images).

**Point**

A Point is a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that holds two [integers](#part0003_split_082.html_integer), usually representing x and y [coordinates](#part0003_split_082.html_coordinates). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_067.html_kp11.6) in [*Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position*](#part0003_split_066.html_Lesson-11.6---Window-Size-and-Position).

**preferred size**

The preferred size of a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) consists of the preferred width and height values (a [Dimension](#part0003_split_082.html_Dimension)) the programmer desired for the [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component). Some [layouts](#part0003_split_082.html_layout) display [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component) at their preferred size, others do not. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_019.html_kp2.3) in [*Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension*](#part0003_split_018.html_Lesson-2.3---Multiple-Panels,-Preferred-Size,-Dimension).

Always provide the preferred size of a [panel](#part0003_split_082.html_panel) that holds no [components](#part0003_split_082.html_component), such as a [panel](#part0003_split_082.html_panel) used as a drawing surface, by overriding the panel's *getPreferredSize()* method. Otherwise, no space may be reserved for that [panel](#part0003_split_082.html_panel) in the [layout](#part0003_split_082.html_layout). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_042.html_kp7.1) in [*Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size*](#part0003_split_041.html_Lesson-7.1---A-Painted-Panel:-Color,-Rectangles,-Lines,-Circles,-and-Preferred-Size).

**primitive**

The Java primitive data [types](#part0003_split_082.html_type) are [int](#part0003_split_082.html_int), [double](#part0003_split_082.html_double), [char](#part0003_split_082.html_character), [boolean](#part0003_split_082.html_boolean), [byte](#part0003_split_082.html_byte), [short](#part0003_split_082.html_short), [long](#part0003_split_082.html_long), and [float](#part0003_split_082.html_float). The primitive [types](#part0003_split_082.html_type) require no [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) [definitions,](#part0003_split_082.html_define) and are manipulated using language-defined operations, rather than by [calling](#part0003_split_082.html_call) a [methods.](#part0003_split_082.html_method) See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 15.5 - Array Lists* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**private**

A [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) or [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) may be [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) as private. A private [declaration](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) means that only [objects](#part0003_split_082.html_object) of the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) the [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) or [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) can see or use the [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) or [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 6.3 - Methods* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**programmer**

A programmer is a person who writes computer program [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code).

**protected**

A [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) or [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) may be [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) as protected. A protected [declaration](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) means that only [objects](#part0003_split_082.html_object) of the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) the [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) or [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method), or [objects](#part0003_split_082.html_object) of any [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) that [extends](#part0003_split_082.html_extend) that [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class), can see or use the [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) or [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**public**

A [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) or [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) may be [declared](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) as public. A public [declaration](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) means an [object](#part0003_split_082.html_object) of any [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) in the same [build path](#part0003_split_082.html_build-path) may see or use the [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) or [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method). See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**Quick Fix**

The Quick Fix feature of Eclipse lists ways Eclipse thinks a [syntax error](#part0003_split_082.html_syntax-error) could be fixed. To use Quick Fix, rest your mouse on the underlined error in the [code](#part0003_split_082.html_code). Eclipse will list ways to fix the problem. Select one of the options and Eclipse will fix the error for you. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**radio button**

A radio button is a [clickable](#part0003_split_082.html_clickable) [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) with text. A radio button has only two states: selected or not selected. Use [JRadioButton](#part0003_split_082.html_JRadioButton) to create radio buttons. Radio buttons are usually added to a [button group](#part0003_split_082.html_button-group), in which only one radio button may be selected at a time. Use [ButtonGroup](#part0003_split_082.html_ButtonGroup) to create button groups. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_056.html_kp10.2) in [*Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons*](#part0003_split_055.html_Lesson-10.2---Text-Fields,-Radio-Buttons).

**random**

If an item in a set is chosen at random, choosing any item is equally likely. See *Key Points and More* in *Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**ratio**

A ratio is a number representing how large one number is compared to the other. For example, if a number is half the size of another number, the numbers have a 1 to 2 ratio. The ratio may be represented as a single number by dividing the two numbers. In other words, the same ratio could be represented as 1/2 or .5\. See [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners).

**repaint**

When a program repaints a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component), the program asks Java to draw the entire [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) again. A [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) should be repainted whenever the program changes [instance variable](#part0003_split_082.html_instance-variable) values that might affect how the [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) should look. Use the [component's](#part0003_split_082.html_component) *repaint()* method to repaint the [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_042.html_kp7.1) in [*Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size*](#part0003_split_041.html_Lesson-7.1---A-Painted-Panel:-Color,-Rectangles,-Lines,-Circles,-and-Preferred-Size).

**reset**

Resetting a [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) returns it to its original value.

**resize**

To resize a [component](#part0003_split_082.html_component) or an image, change its size to a new size. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_049.html_kp8.4) in [*Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image*](#part0003_split_048.html_Lesson-8.4---New-Graphics,-Scale-an-Image). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_066.html_kp11.5) in [*Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window*](#part0003_split_065.html_Lesson-11.5---Component-Listeners,-Window-State-Listeners,-Resize-a-Window). See [*Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners*](#part0003_split_071.html_Lesson-12.3---Focus-Listeners).

**resolved**

Getting an error that a [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) name cannot be resolved means that Java doesn't know how the [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) is [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define). This error is usually fixed by [declaring](#part0003_split_082.html_declare) the [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) before the [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) is used. See *Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*

Getting an error that a [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) name cannot be resolved means that Java doesn't know how the [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class) is [defined](#part0003_split_082.html_define). This error is usually fixed by using [Quick Fix](#part0003_split_082.html_Quick-Fix) to [import](#part0003_split_082.html_import) the needed [class](#part0003_split_082.html_class).. See *Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers* in *Do-It-Yourself Java Games*.

**resource**

A program's resources include any additional files that are needed for the program to [run](#part0003_split_082.html_run). The resources often include data files and image files. See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_068.html_kp11.7) in [*Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File*](#part0003_split_067.html_Lesson-11.7---Put-Data-Files-in-the-JAR-File). See [*Key Points and More*](#part0003_split_070.html_kp12.1) in [*Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars*](#part0003_split_069.html_Lesson-12.1---Toolbars).

**respectively**

The word “respectively” is often used in this book when referring to a list of [variables](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) and a list of their initial values. To set the [variables](#part0003_split_082.html_variable) to their values, respectively, means to assign the first value to the first [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable), the second value to the second [variable](#part0003_split_082.html_variable), etc.

**return**

A [method](#part0003_split_082.html_method) may optionally return a value.
